blocks.html: In Algebra 1 you solved two equations in two unknowns by eliminating one of them. Linear algebra starts from that same skill, then asks a bigger question: what does a system look like, and what kinds of answers can it have? There are two useful pictures, and you will use both for the rest of the course.

A linear equation in the unknowns $x_1, \dots, x_n$ has the form $a_1x_1 + a_2x_2 + \cdots + a_nx_n = b$, where the $a_i$ and $b$ are numbers. No products of unknowns, no powers, no square roots. A system is a list of such equations, and a solution is a list of numbers $(s_1, \dots, s_n)$ that makes every equation true at once. The set of all solutions is the solution set.

blocks.text: The row picture: lines and planes

blocks.html: Take the system $2x - y = 1$ and $x + y = 5$. Each equation, on its own, is a line in the $xy$-plane: all the points that satisfy it. A solution must lie on both lines, so it is where they cross. Drag the probe point and watch which equations it satisfies.

opts.task: Drag the probe to the point that satisfies both equations.

blocks.cap: Row picture: each equation is a line; the solution is where they meet.

blocks.html: With three unknowns, each equation is a plane in space. Three planes can meet in a single point, share a whole line, or have no point in common (for example, two of them parallel).

Now read the same system down the columns. The coefficients of $x$ form the vector $\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$ and those of $y$ form $\begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$. The system says $$x\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + y\begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}.$$ So the question becomes: how much of each column vector do we need to reach the right-hand side? This uses exactly the scaling and adding of vectors from precalculus.

blocks.title: Both pictures for one system
blocks.q: Solve $2x - y = 1$, $x + y = 5$, and check the answer in both pictures.
steps: Add the two equations: the $y$ terms cancel, leaving $3x = 6$, so $x = 2$.
Row picture check: $(2, 3)$ is on both lines, since $2(2) - 3 = 1$ and $2 + 3 = 5$.

blocks.title: A system with no solution
blocks.q: How many solutions does $x + 2y = 3$, $2x + 4y = 7$ have?
steps: Double the first equation: $2x + 4y = 6$. The second equation has the same left side but says it equals $7$.
No pair $(x, y)$ can make $2x + 4y$ equal both $6$ and $7$. The lines have the same slope and different intercepts: they are parallel.

Column picture: the columns $\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}$ point along the same line through the origin, and $\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}$ is not on that line, so no combination reaches it.

blocks.html: Why can a linear system never have exactly two solutions? Suppose $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$ are two different solutions. For any number $t$, look at $\mathbf{p} + t(\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{p})$. In each equation $a_1x_1 + \cdots + a_nx_n = b$, the left side is linear, so plugging in this point gives $b + t(b - b) = b$. Every one of these infinitely many points is a solution. So once there are two, there are infinitely many.

blocks.html: In precalculus you solved systems with row operations. Here we make that tool precise, because the whole course rests on it. The first step is to stop copying the letters: in a system, only the numbers carry information.

For the system $$\begin{aligned} x + 2y - z &= 4 \\ 2x - y + 3z &= 9 \\ -x + y + z &= 0 \end{aligned}$$ the coefficient matrix collects the coefficients, one row per equation and one column per unknown, and the augmented matrix adds the constants as a last column: $$\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ 2 & -1 & 3 & 9 \\ -1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \end{array}\right]$$ The bar is a reminder that the last column holds the right-hand sides. A missing unknown has coefficient $0$, and every row must list the unknowns in the same order.

items: Replacement: add a multiple of one row to a different row. Written $R_2 \to R_2 - 2R_1$: "replace row 2 by row 2 minus twice row 1".
Scaling: multiply every entry of a row by a nonzero number: $R_3 \to \frac{1}{2}R_3$.
Interchange: swap two rows: $R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2$.

blocks.html: Each operation can be undone by another operation of the same kind: $R_2 \to R_2 - 2R_1$ is undone by $R_2 \to R_2 + 2R_1$, scaling by $c$ is undone by scaling by $\frac{1}{c}$, and a swap undoes itself. Now, any solution of the old system also solves the new one, because the new equations are built from true equations by adding and multiplying. Since we can go back, any solution of the new system solves the old one too. So the solution set never changes. Matrices that are connected by row operations are called row equivalent, and their systems have exactly the same solutions.

opts.task: Apply $R_2 \to R_2 - 3R_1$ and watch the gold point. Then try scaling a row by $0$ and see what goes wrong.

blocks.cap: Each row is a line. Legal row operations change the lines but never the point where they cross.

blocks.title: Writing the augmented matrix
blocks.q: Write the augmented matrix of $3y - x = 2$, $x + 4z = -1$, $2x - y + z = 5$, with columns $x, y, z$.
steps: Rewrite each equation with the unknowns in order: $-x + 3y + 0z = 2$, then $x + 0y + 4z = -1$, then $2x - y + z = 5$.
Copy the coefficients row by row and put the constants after the bar: $\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} -1 & 3 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 4 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 & 5 \end{array}\right]$

blocks.title: Two replacements
blocks.q: Apply $R_2 \to R_2 - 2R_1$ and then $R_3 \to R_3 + R_1$ to $\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ 2 & -1 & 3 & 9 \\ -1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \end{array}\right]$.
steps: Row 2 minus twice row 1, entry by entry: $(2 - 2,\; -1 - 4,\; 3 + 2 \mid 9 - 8)$ $= (0, -5, 5 \mid 1)$. Rows 1 and 3 do not change: $\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ 0 & -5 & 5 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \end{array}\right]$
The new system has the same solutions as the old one, and it is simpler: $x$ now appears only in the first equation.

blocks.html: Two moves look like row operations but are not: multiplying a row by $0$, and replacing a row by itself minus itself ($R_1 \to R_1 - R_1$). Both turn the row into zeros, which throws away an equation and can add solutions. Copying one row over another ($R_2 \to R_1$) also loses an equation. (Adding a row to itself, $R_1 \to R_1 + R_1$, is harmless: that is just scaling by $2$.) Quick check: ask "can I undo this?" If not, it is not allowed.
Always change the row named on the left of the arrow, and only that row. The row you use as a tool stays the same.

An augmented matrix is a system with the letters removed. Replacement, nonzero scaling and interchange are reversible, so they never change the solution set; that is what lets us simplify a system without losing or gaining solutions.

blocks.html: Row operations, from the last topic, can change a system as much as we like without changing its solutions. So which shape should we aim for? A staircase.

In each nonzero row, the first nonzero entry is its leading entry. A matrix is in echelon form when (1) all rows of zeros are at the bottom, and (2) each leading entry is in a column to the right of the leading entry in the row above. Then every entry below a leading entry is $0$. The leading entries' positions are called pivot positions, and their columns are pivot columns.

$$\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 4 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \text{ is in echelon form;} \quad \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \text{ is not.}$$ In the second matrix, the $3$ sits below the first pivot.

items: Find the leftmost column that is not all zeros. Its top entry (after a swap, if needed) is the pivot.
Use replacements to make every entry below the pivot $0$.
Cover the pivot row and repeat on the rows below it, until you run out of rows or columns.
Back-substitute: solve the last equation, then work upward.

blocks.html: Why does this always work, and why is the result easy? Each round clears one column below a pivot, and later rounds only use rows that already have zeros in the earlier columns, so they never spoil earlier work. At the end, the last nonzero equation has the fewest unknowns, often just one. Each equation above it brings in one new unknown, so back substitution solves for one unknown at a time.

opts.task: Reduce this matrix to echelon form. Use your own steps, or press "Next step for me" to watch.

blocks.cap: Elimination on the system from the first example.

blocks.title: Elimination and back substitution
steps: Clear below the first pivot. Row 3 already has a $0$ there. $R_{2} \to R_{2} + R_{1}$: $\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 1 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & -2 & 3 & -10 \\ 0 & -4 & 5 & -18 \end{array}\right]$
Clear below the second pivot, $-2$: $R_{3} \to R_{3} - 2R_{2}$: $\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 1 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & -2 & 3 & -10 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 2 \end{array}\right]$. Echelon form.

blocks.title: When fractions appear
steps: The pivot is $2$ and the entry below it is $3$, so the multiplier is $\frac{3}{2}$: $R_{2} \to R_{2} - \frac{3}{2}R_{1}$ gives $\left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 2 & 3 & 8 \\ 0 & -\frac{11}{2} & -11 \end{array}\right]$.
Row 2 says $-\frac{11}{2}y = -11$. Multiply both sides by $-\frac{2}{11}$: $y = 2$.
Check in both original equations: $2(1) + 3(2) = 8$ ✓ and $3(1) - 2 = 1$ ✓.
To dodge the fractions you could first scale ($R_2 \to 2R_2$), then use $R_2 \to R_2 - 3R_1$. Both routes give the same answer.

blocks.html: Small slips with signs and fractions are the most common error in elimination, and they are invisible unless you check. Always substitute your answer into every original equation, not the reduced ones: an error made during elimination is built into the reduced system, so it would pass that check.

Echelon form is a staircase: zeros below each pivot, each pivot to the right of the one above. Gaussian elimination reaches it with replacements (and swaps when a pivot is $0$), and back substitution then solves from the bottom up.

blocks.html: Echelon form is good enough for back substitution, but it is not unique: different sequences of row operations give different staircases. One more round of simplifying gives a form that is unique and lets you read the solution with no back substitution at all.

A matrix is in reduced row echelon form (RREF) when it is in echelon form and also (3) every pivot is $1$, and (4) each pivot is the only nonzero entry in its column. For example, $$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 3 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$$ is in RREF: columns 1, 2 and 4 hold the pivots, and each of those columns is a single $1$ with zeros above and below.

First reach echelon form as before (the forward phase). Then, starting with the rightmost pivot and moving left, scale each pivot row so the pivot is $1$ and use replacements to clear the entries above it (the backward phase).

Why go right to left? When you clear above the pivot in column $j$, you add multiples of its row to the rows above. That row has zeros in every column to the left of $j$, so it cannot disturb the pivots already sitting in those columns. And the payoff: in RREF, each nonzero row contains exactly one pivot unknown, so each equation reads "pivot unknown $=$ number (minus free terms)". The fact that every matrix has exactly one RREF, whatever steps you take, is a theorem we will use often; it means the RREF is a fingerprint of the matrix.

blocks.title: From a system to its RREF
blocks.q: Find the RREF of $\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 2 & 1 & 4 \\ 2 & 5 & 4 & 11 \\ -1 & -1 & 2 & 1 \end{array}\right]$.
steps: Forward: $R_{2} \to R_{2} - 2R_{1}$ and $R_{3} \to R_{3} + R_{1}$ clear column 1: $\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 2 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 5 \end{array}\right]$
$R_{3} \to R_{3} - R_{2}$ clears below the second pivot: $\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 2 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 \end{array}\right]$. Echelon form, with pivots $1, 1, 1$.

Backward, starting at the right: $R_{1} \to R_{1} - R_{3}$ and $R_{2} \to R_{2} - 2R_{3}$ clear above the third pivot: $\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 2 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 \end{array}\right]$
$R_{1} \to R_{1} - 2R_{2}$ clears above the second pivot: $\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 0 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 \end{array}\right]$
Read the solution: $x = 4$, $y = -1$, $z = 2$. Check in row 2 of the original: $2(4) + 5(-1) + 4(2) = 11$. ✓

blocks.title: Scaling a pivot to 1
blocks.q: Find the RREF of $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 & -2 & 6 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 & 7 \end{bmatrix}$.
steps: $R_{2} \to R_{2} - R_{1}$: $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$. The second pivot is already $1$.

blocks.html: Software uses RREF for small problems; for big ones it stops at echelon form, because the backward phase costs extra arithmetic. By hand, RREF is worth it when you need to describe all solutions.
RREF is echelon form plus two rules: every pivot is $1$, and every pivot is alone in its column. Each matrix has exactly one RREF, and from it you can read the solutions directly.

blocks.html: When the reduced echelon form has a column without a pivot, the system does not pin down every unknown. This topic is about describing all the solutions in that case, clearly and completely.

An unknown whose column holds a pivot is a basic variable. The others are free variables. Each nonzero row of the RREF contains exactly one basic variable, so each row can be solved for its basic variable in terms of the free ones.

Why may a free variable take any value? Its column has no pivot, so no row "belongs" to it: no equation forces its value. Whatever numbers you choose for the free variables, each pivot row then gives exactly one value for its basic variable. So every choice of the free variables gives one solution, and every solution arises this way.

blocks.title: One free variable
blocks.q: The augmented matrix of a system in $x_1, x_2, x_3$ reduces to $\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 0 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -1 \end{array}\right]$. Describe all solutions.
steps: Pivots are in columns 1 and 2, so $x_1, x_2$ are basic and $x_3$ is free. Call it $x_3 = t$.
All solutions: $(x_1, x_2, x_3)$ $= (3 + 2t,\; -1 - t,\; t)$ for every real $t$.
In vector form: $\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ -1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + t\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$, a line in $\mathbb{R}^3$ through $(3, -1, 0)$ in the direction $(2, -1, 1)$.

blocks.title: Two free variables
blocks.q: Describe all solutions of the system whose augmented matrix reduces to $\left[\begin{array}{cccc|c} 1 & 3 & 0 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5 & -1 \end{array}\right]$ (unknowns $x_1, \dots, x_4$).
steps: Pivots in columns 1 and 3: $x_1, x_3$ are basic; $x_2 = s$ and $x_4 = t$ are free.

$\mathbf{x}$ $= \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 0 \\ -1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + s\begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + t\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ -5 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$: a plane of solutions inside $\mathbb{R}^4$.

opts.task: Drag the probe along the line. Every point on it satisfies both equations.

blocks.cap: The two equations describe the same line. With $y = t$ free, the solutions are $(4 - 2t, t)$: one point for each $t$.

blocks.html: Setting the free variables to $0$ and reporting that single point as "the solution". It is a solution (for the line above, $(4, 0)$), but the question asks for all of them, and there are infinitely many. Check: if your answer has no letter in it while some column had no pivot, something is missing.

The constant vector (here $(3, -1, 0)$) is the solution with every free variable equal to $0$. The vectors multiplying the parameters will turn out to solve the system with all constants replaced by $0$. That pattern is coming soon, in homogeneous systems.

Basic variables (pivot columns) are solved for; free variables (no pivot) are parameters that can be anything. The general solution writes every unknown in terms of the parameters, often as $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{p} + t\mathbf{v}$ (+ more terms for more free variables).

blocks.html: Two questions come before solving: does a solution exist (is the system consistent)? And if so, is it unique? Once a matrix is in echelon form, both answers can be read from the pivot positions, often without finishing the solution. This builds on free variables.

items: A system is consistent exactly when the last column of the augmented matrix is not a pivot column, that is, when the echelon form has no row $\left[\,0\ \cdots\ 0 \mid b\,\right]$ with $b \neq 0$.

If it is consistent, the solution is unique when every column of the coefficient matrix is a pivot column (no free variables), and there are infinitely many solutions when at least one variable is free.

blocks.html: A row $\left[\,0\ 0\ \cdots\ 0 \mid b\,\right]$ stands for the equation $0x_1 + \cdots + 0x_n = b$, which says $0 = b$. If $b \neq 0$, no choice of unknowns makes it true, and since row operations keep the solution set, the original system has no solution either. If there is no such row, back substitution never gets stuck: give the free variables any values and solve upward. No free variables means one solution; any free variable means one solution for each of its infinitely many values.

blocks.title: Reading three echelon forms
blocks.q: How many solutions? $$\text{(a) } \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 4 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & 6 \end{array}\right] \quad \text{(b) } \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 4 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 6 \end{array}\right] \quad \text{(c) } \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 4 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array}\right]$$
steps: (a) No row of the form $[\,0\ 0\ 0 \mid b\,]$. Pivots in all three variable columns: no free variables. Exactly one solution.
(c) Row 3 says $0 = 0$, which is always true; it just tells us one equation was redundant. Column 3 has no pivot, so $x_3$ is free: infinitely many solutions.

blocks.title: A parameter in the system
blocks.q: For which $h$ is the system with augmented matrix $\left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & -3 & 2 \\ -2 & 6 & h \end{array}\right]$ consistent?
steps: Row 2 says $0 = h + 4$. That is possible only when $h = -4$.
For $h = -4$ the second row is all zeros and $y$ is free, so there are infinitely many solutions. For every other $h$, none.

blocks.html: "There is a row of zeros, so there is no solution." Not so. A row that is zero everywhere, including after the bar, says $0 = 0$: harmless. Only a row that is zero on the left and nonzero after the bar means no solution. Check: read the row aloud as an equation.

blocks.html: The column picture turned a system into a question about combining vectors. This topic sets up the language for that, in any number of dimensions.

A vector in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is an ordered list of $n$ real numbers, written as a column: $\mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} v_1 \\ \vdots \\ v_n \end{bmatrix}$. Two vectors are equal when every entry matches. We add vectors entry by entry and multiply a vector by a number (a scalar) by multiplying every entry. For $n = 2$ or $3$ you can draw them as arrows from the origin; for larger $n$ the algebra works the same even though the picture runs out.

In the plane, adding $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}$ means walking along $\mathbf{u}$ and then along $\mathbf{v}$ (tip to tail); the sum is the diagonal of the parallelogram the two arrows make. Scaling by $c$ stretches an arrow by $|c|$ and flips it when $c < 0$. The usual rules hold because they hold in each entry: $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{u}$, $c(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) = c\mathbf{u} + c\mathbf{v}$, $(c + d)\mathbf{u} = c\mathbf{u} + d\mathbf{u}$, and $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{u}$.

Given vectors $\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_p$ and scalars $c_1, \dots, c_p$, the vector $$c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + c_2\mathbf{v}_2 + \cdots + c_p\mathbf{v}_p$$ is a linear combination of the $\mathbf{v}$'s with weights $c_1, \dots, c_p$. Weights can be any real numbers, including $0$ and negatives.

blocks.title: Computing a combination
blocks.q: Let $\mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}$. Compute $3\mathbf{u} - 2\mathbf{v}$.

blocks.html: Why is "is $\mathbf{b}$ a combination of $\mathbf{a}_1, \dots, \mathbf{a}_p$?" a question about a linear system? Write $x_1\mathbf{a}_1 + \cdots + x_p\mathbf{a}_p = \mathbf{b}$ and compare entry $i$ on both sides: it says $x_1a_{i1} + \cdots + x_pa_{ip} = b_i$, a linear equation. All the entries together form a system whose augmented matrix is $[\,\mathbf{a}_1\ \cdots\ \mathbf{a}_p \mid \mathbf{b}\,]$. So $\mathbf{b}$ is a combination exactly when that system is consistent, and the solutions are the weights.

blocks.title: Finding the weights
blocks.q: Is $\mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}$ a linear combination of $\mathbf{a}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{a}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}$? If so, find the weights.
steps: $R_3 \to R_3 - 2R_1$ gives row 3 $= (0, -5 \mid 5)$; then $R_3 \to R_3 + 5R_2$ gives $(0, 0 \mid 0)$; then $R_1 \to R_1 - 2R_2$: $\left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array}\right]$.

blocks.html: The zero vector is a combination of any vectors (all weights $0$), and each $\mathbf{v}_i$ is a combination of the set (weight $1$ on it, $0$ on the rest). Vectors with many entries are everyday objects: a store's sales of 50 products in one week is a vector in $\mathbb{R}^{50}$, and the sales over a month are a combination of the weekly vectors with weights $1$.

A linear combination scales vectors and adds them. Asking whether $\mathbf{b}$ is a combination of $\mathbf{a}_1, \dots, \mathbf{a}_p$ is the same as asking whether the system with augmented matrix $[\,\mathbf{a}_1\ \cdots\ \mathbf{a}_p \mid \mathbf{b}\,]$ has a solution.

blocks.html: Collect every linear combination of a set of vectors and you get its span: $$\operatorname{Span}\{\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_p\} = \{\,c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \cdots + c_p\mathbf{v}_p : c_1, \dots, c_p \text{ real}\,\}.$$ It always contains $\mathbf{0}$ and each $\mathbf{v}_i$. The span is everywhere you can reach using only those directions.

items: The span of one nonzero vector is the line through the origin in its direction.
The span of two vectors that are not multiples of each other is a plane through the origin. In $\mathbb{R}^2$ that plane is all of $\mathbb{R}^2$; in $\mathbb{R}^3$ it is a flat sheet.
If one vector is a multiple of the other, the second adds no new direction: the span is still a line.

blocks.title: Is b in the span?
blocks.q: Is $\mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 4 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$ in $\operatorname{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2\}$ with $\mathbf{a}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{a}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$?
steps: $R_2 \to R_2 + R_1$ and $R_3 \to R_3 - 2R_1$: rows 2 and 3 become $(0, 3 \mid 6)$ and $(0, -5 \mid -3)$.
Inconsistent, so $\mathbf{b}$ is not in the span. Geometrically, $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ span a plane in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and $\mathbf{b}$ is off it.

blocks.title: Choosing h to land in the span
blocks.q: For which $h$ is $\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 1 \\ h \end{bmatrix}$ in $\operatorname{Span}\left\{\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\right\}$?
steps: The first two entries do not involve $h$: $x_1 + x_2 = 5$ and $x_2 = 1$, so $x_2 = 1$ and $x_1 = 4$.
The third entry must then agree: $h = 2x_1 + x_2 = 8 + 1 = 9$.
For any other $h$ the last row of the reduced augmented matrix reads $0 = h - 9 \neq 0$.

blocks.html: When do the columns of $A$ (an $m \times n$ matrix) span all of $\mathbb{R}^m$? Exactly when $A$ has a pivot in every row. If every row has a pivot, no row of the echelon form can become $[\,0 \cdots 0 \mid c\,]$, so every $\mathbf{b}$ is reachable. If some row has no pivot, the echelon form has a zero row; put a $1$ after the bar in that row and run the row operations backward to build a $\mathbf{b}$ that cannot be reached.

"Two vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ span $\mathbb{R}^3$." They cannot. The matrix with them as columns is $3 \times 2$, so it has at most 2 pivots, but spanning $\mathbb{R}^3$ needs a pivot in all 3 rows. Two independent vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ span a plane. In general you need at least $m$ vectors to span $\mathbb{R}^m$, and having $m$ of them is not enough on its own.

The span is the set of all linear combinations. $\mathbf{b}$ is in the span of the columns of $A$ exactly when $[\,A \mid \mathbf{b}\,]$ is consistent, and the columns span all of $\mathbb{R}^m$ exactly when $A$ has a pivot in every row.

blocks.html: We have been writing systems as combinations of columns. A matrix-vector product packs that into two symbols. It is the single most important definition in the course.

If $A$ is $m \times n$ with columns $\mathbf{a}_1, \dots, \mathbf{a}_n$, and $\mathbf{x}$ is in $\mathbb{R}^n$, then $$A\mathbf{x} = x_1\mathbf{a}_1 + x_2\mathbf{a}_2 + \cdots + x_n\mathbf{a}_n.$$ The entries of $\mathbf{x}$ are the weights on the columns. So $\mathbf{x}$ must have exactly one entry per column of $A$, and the result lives in $\mathbb{R}^m$, like the columns.

blocks.title: Two ways to compute Ax
blocks.q: Compute $A\mathbf{x}$ for $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$.
steps: By rows (faster by hand): entry $i$ is row $i$ of $A$ times $\mathbf{x}$, entry by entry, added up. Entry 1: $(1)(3) + (2)(1) + (-1)(2)$ $= 3$. Entry 2: $(0)(3) + (-3)(1) + (4)(2)$ $= 5$.
Both give $\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}$: $A$ is $2 \times 3$, $\mathbf{x}$ has 3 entries, and $A\mathbf{x}$ has 2.

blocks.html: So one system has three equivalent forms: a list of equations, a vector equation $x_1\mathbf{a}_1 + \cdots + x_n\mathbf{a}_n = \mathbf{b}$, and the matrix equation $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$. All three have the same solutions, and $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has a solution exactly when $\mathbf{b}$ is in the span of the columns of $A$.

blocks.name: matrix2d

opts.task: Drag $\mathbf{v}$. Notice that $A\mathbf{v}$ is always $v_1$ times the green column plus $v_2$ times the red one.

blocks.cap: The columns of $A$ are $A\hat{\imath}$ and $A\hat{\jmath}$; every $A\mathbf{v}$ is a combination of them.

blocks.html: $A$ respects sums and multiples: $A(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) = A\mathbf{u} + A\mathbf{v}$ and $A(c\mathbf{u}) = cA\mathbf{u}$. Proof from the definition: $A(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v})$ $= (u_1 + v_1)\mathbf{a}_1 + \cdots + (u_n + v_n)\mathbf{a}_n$, and regrouping gives $(u_1\mathbf{a}_1 + \cdots) + (v_1\mathbf{a}_1 + \cdots)$ $= A\mathbf{u} + A\mathbf{v}$. Scaling is the same idea. These two facts will become the definition of a linear map.

One matrix deserves a name now. The identity matrix $I_n$ has $1$s on the diagonal and $0$s elsewhere, so its columns are $\mathbf{e}_1, \dots, \mathbf{e}_n$, and $I_n\mathbf{x} = x_1\mathbf{e}_1 + \cdots + x_n\mathbf{e}_n = \mathbf{x}$ for every $\mathbf{x}$. Likewise $A\mathbf{e}_j$ is simply column $j$ of $A$: a handy way to pull out a column.

blocks.title: From a system to Ax = b
blocks.q: Write $3x_1 - x_2 = 4$, $x_1 + 5x_3 = 0$ as a matrix equation.
steps: Unknowns $x_1, x_2, x_3$ give three columns; a missing unknown gets a $0$.

blocks.html: Multiplying entries of $\mathbf{x}$ against the columns in the wrong pattern (for example, row 1 of $A$ times row 1 of $\mathbf{x}$ only), or trying to multiply when sizes do not match. Check: $\mathbf{x}$ needs as many entries as $A$ has columns, and $A\mathbf{x}$ has as many entries as $A$ has rows. A $2 \times 3$ matrix times a vector with 2 entries is not defined.
$A\mathbf{x}$ is the combination of the columns of $A$ with the entries of $\mathbf{x}$ as weights. So $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ is solvable exactly when $\mathbf{b}$ is in the span of the columns.

blocks.html: A system $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$, with every constant equal to zero, is called homogeneous. It always has at least one solution, $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$, called the trivial solution. So existence is never in doubt; the real question is whether there are others. This uses free variables and the matrix equation.

$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ has a nontrivial solution exactly when the equation has at least one free variable, that is, when some column of $A$ has no pivot. Its solution set is the span of one vector per free variable.

blocks.title: Parametric vector form
blocks.q: Solve $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ for $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 5 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.
steps: Row reduce $A$ (the column of zeros never changes, so leave it off): $R_2 \to R_2 - 2R_1$ gives $(0, 1, 3)$, then $R_1 \to R_1 - 2R_2$: $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -7 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$.
$x_3$ is free; let $x_3 = t$. Row 1: $x_1 = 7t$. Row 2: $x_2 = -3t$.

$\mathbf{x} = t\begin{bmatrix} 7 \\ -3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$. The solution set is $\operatorname{Span}\left\{\begin{bmatrix} 7 \\ -3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\right\}$: a line through the origin in $\mathbb{R}^3$.

blocks.name: matrix2d

opts.task: Drag $\mathbf{v}$ until $A\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$. Which line are you on?

blocks.cap: This $A$ squashes the plane onto a line. Every vector on the line through $(2, -1)$ is sent to $\mathbf{0}$: those are the solutions of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$.

blocks.html: Compare the general solution of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ from the parametric topic, $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{p} + t\mathbf{v}$, with the solution of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$: the same $t\mathbf{v}$ appears. That is no accident.

Suppose $A\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{b}$. If $A\mathbf{v}_h = \mathbf{0}$, then $A(\mathbf{p} + \mathbf{v}_h)$ $= A\mathbf{p} + A\mathbf{v}_h$ $= \mathbf{b} + \mathbf{0}$ $= \mathbf{b}$, so $\mathbf{p} + \mathbf{v}_h$ is a solution. Conversely, if $A\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{b}$, then $A(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{p}) = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{0}$, so $\mathbf{y}$ $= \mathbf{p} + (\text{a homogeneous solution})$. Every solution of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ is one particular solution plus a solution of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$. Geometrically, the solution set of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ is the solution set of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ slid over by $\mathbf{p}$: a parallel line or plane.

blocks.title: Using the structure
blocks.q: For the same $A$, one solution of $A\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$ is $\mathbf{p} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ -1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$. Find all solutions.
steps: All solutions are $\mathbf{p}$ plus the homogeneous solutions: $\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ -1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + t\begin{bmatrix} 7 \\ -3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$.

blocks.html: With one free variable the homogeneous solutions form a line through the origin; with two, a plane through the origin; in general, the span of one vector for each free variable. Those vectors come straight from the reduced echelon form: set one free variable to $1$ and the others to $0$, and read off the basic variables. We will meet this set again under the name null space.
If $A$ has more columns than rows, $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ always has a nontrivial solution: there are more unknowns than possible pivots, so something is free.

blocks.html: Some sets of vectors contain a redundant member: one that the others can already build. Independence is the precise way to say there is no redundancy. It rests on homogeneous systems.

Vectors $\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_p$ are linearly independent if the only way to make $$c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + c_2\mathbf{v}_2 + \cdots + c_p\mathbf{v}_p = \mathbf{0}$$ is with every $c_i = 0$. Otherwise they are linearly dependent, and a choice of weights, not all zero, that gives $\mathbf{0}$ is a dependence relation.
The columns of $A$ are independent exactly when $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ has only the trivial solution, that is, when every column of $A$ has a pivot.

Dependent means some vector is a combination of the others. If $c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \cdots + c_p\mathbf{v}_p = \mathbf{0}$ with, say, $c_j 
eq 0$, divide by $c_j$ and solve for $\mathbf{v}_j$: it equals a combination of the rest. Conversely, if $\mathbf{v}_j = \sum_{i 
eq j} a_i\mathbf{v}_i$, then $\sum_{i 
eq j} a_i\mathbf{v}_i - \mathbf{v}_j = \mathbf{0}$ is a dependence relation (the weight on $\mathbf{v}_j$ is $-1 
eq 0$). So dependent means "redundant": removing that vector does not shrink the span.

blocks.title: Three vectors, none a multiple of another
blocks.q: Are $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 5 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{v}_3 = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$ independent? If not, find a dependence relation.
steps: Put them in the columns of $A$ and row reduce: $A$ $= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 5 & 1 \\ 3 & 6 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \to \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$.
Column 3 has no pivot, so $x_3$ is free: the vectors are dependent.

blocks.html: Checking only pairs. In the example, no vector is a multiple of another, yet the set is dependent: $\mathbf{v}_3$ is built from $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$ together. The pair test works only for two vectors. For three or more, row reduce and look for a free variable.

Geometrically, in $\mathbb{R}^3$: two vectors are independent when they point along different lines; three are independent when they do not all lie in one plane through the origin. Independent vectors each add a new direction, so the span grows by one dimension with each of them.

items: Two vectors are dependent exactly when one is a multiple of the other.
Any set containing $\mathbf{0}$ is dependent ($1\cdot\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}$ is a dependence relation).
More vectors than entries ($p > n$ vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$) is always dependent: the $n \times p$ matrix has more columns than rows, so some column has no pivot.

blocks.title: No computation needed
blocks.q: Are $\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}$ independent?
steps: Three vectors in $\mathbb{R}^2$: the matrix is $2 \times 3$, with at most 2 pivots for 3 columns.
A free variable must exist, so the set is dependent.

blocks.cap: When $\mathbf{v}$ is a multiple of $\mathbf{u}$, the two vectors are dependent and their span is only a line. Drag a tip off the line to make them independent: the span jumps to the whole plane.

blocks.html: You multiplied matrices in precalculus with a row-times-column rule. Here we see where that rule comes from, which explains its strange features: sizes must match, and order matters.

Sums and scalar multiples work entry by entry (for matrices of the same size). The product is defined so that multiplying by $AB$ does the same as multiplying by $B$ and then by $A$: $$(AB)\mathbf{x} = A(B\mathbf{x}) \text{ for every } \mathbf{x}.$$ That forces the definition $AB$ $= [\,A\mathbf{b}_1\ A\mathbf{b}_2\ \cdots\ A\mathbf{b}_p\,]$: column $j$ of $AB$ is $A$ times column $j$ of $B$.

Why must column $j$ of $AB$ be $A\mathbf{b}_j$? Take $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{e}_j$ (all zeros except a $1$ in entry $j$). Then $B\mathbf{e}_j = \mathbf{b}_j$, so $(AB)\mathbf{e}_j = A\mathbf{b}_j$, and $(AB)\mathbf{e}_j$ is column $j$ of $AB$. Writing out $A\mathbf{b}_j$ with the row rule gives the familiar formula: entry $(i, j)$ of $AB$ is row $i$ of $A$ times column $j$ of $B$. And it explains the size rule: $A$ ($m \times n$) can only multiply vectors with $n$ entries, so $B$ needs $n$ rows; then $AB$ is $m \times p$.

blocks.title: A product, column by column
blocks.q: Compute $AB$ for $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$.
steps: $A$ is $2 \times 3$ and $B$ is $3 \times 2$: inside sizes match (3), so $AB$ is $2 \times 2$.

blocks.title: Order matters
blocks.q: Compare $CD$ and $DC$ for $C = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $D = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.
steps: They differ. Even when both products exist and have the same size, $AB$ and $BA$ are usually different.

Does not hold in general

blocks.html: The transpose $A^{T}$ turns the rows of $A$ into columns. The product rule reverses the order: $(AB)^{T} = B^{T}A^{T}$. Sizes explain it: if $A$ is $2 \times 3$ and $B$ is $3 \times 2$, then $A^{T}B^{T}$ is $(3 \times 2)(3 \times 2)$, which is not even defined, while $B^{T}A^{T}$ is $(2 \times 3)(3 \times 2)$, which is. Entry $(i, j)$ of $(AB)^{T}$ is entry $(j, i)$ of $AB$: row $j$ of $A$ times column $i$ of $B$, which is row $i$ of $B^{T}$ times column $j$ of $A^{T}$.

Assuming $AB = BA$, or writing $(AB)^{T} = A^{T}B^{T}$. Matrices are actions, and doing $B$ then $A$ is usually not the same as $A$ then $B$ (put on socks, then shoes). Quick check for the transpose rule: test the sizes with a non-square example; the wrong order is not even defined.

blocks.cap: Each matrix is an action on the plane. Try a shear, then a rotation, and compare with the rotation first: the results differ, which is why $AB \neq BA$.

blocks.html: Matrix multiplication is defined so that $(AB)\mathbf{x} = A(B\mathbf{x})$: column $j$ of $AB$ is $A\mathbf{b}_j$. It is associative and distributive but not commutative, and transposes reverse products: $(AB)^{T} = B^{T}A^{T}$.

blocks.html: Numbers have reciprocals: $5 \cdot \frac{1}{5} = 1$. Some square matrices have something similar. You met inverses in precalculus; here we see why the row-reduction method works and how inverses combine. We use reduced echelon form and matrix products.

An $n \times n$ matrix $A$ is invertible if there is a matrix $A^{-1}$ with $AA^{-1} = I$ and $A^{-1}A = I$, where $I$ is the identity matrix. Then $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has exactly one solution, $\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$, for every $\mathbf{b}$.

For a $2 \times 2$ matrix: $$\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{bmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{bmatrix}, \quad \text{provided } ad - bc \neq 0.$$ If $ad - bc = 0$ the matrix has no inverse.

Column $j$ of $A^{-1}$ is the vector $\mathbf{x}_j$ with $A\mathbf{x}_j = \mathbf{e}_j$ (because $AA^{-1} = I$). Solving all $n$ of these systems at once means row reducing $A$ with all the $\mathbf{e}_j$ attached: $[\,A \mid I\,]$. If $A$ reduces to $I$, each system has its unique solution sitting on the right: $[\,I \mid A^{-1}\,]$. If $A$ does not reduce to $I$, some system has no solution or a free variable, and $A$ has no inverse.

blocks.title: A 3 × 3 inverse
blocks.q: Find $A^{-1}$ for $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 5 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.
steps: The left half is $I$, so the right half is $A^{-1}$. Check one entry of $AA^{-1}$: row 1 of $A$ times column 1 of $A^{-1}$ is $(1)(-3) + (2)(2) + (0)(-4)$ $= 1$. ✓

blocks.title: A 2 × 2 inverse and a system
blocks.q: Solve $3x + 5y = 1$, $x + 2y = 0$ using an inverse.

blocks.html: Writing $(AB)^{-1} = A^{-1}B^{-1}$. To undo "do $B$, then $A$", you undo $A$ first and $B$ second, just as you take off your shoes before your socks. Check by multiplying: $(AB)(A^{-1}B^{-1})$ does not collapse, because $B$ and $A^{-1}$ are not next to each other.

blocks.name: matrix2d
blocks.cap: An invertible matrix moves the grid without collapsing it (area factor $\neq 0$), so every point can be traced back. Try the "Squash" preset: the plane flattens onto a line, and no inverse can undo that.

blocks.html: $A^{-1}$ undoes $A$. Row reduce $[\,A \mid I\,]$: if the left side becomes $I$, the right side is $A^{-1}$; if not, $A$ is not invertible. Products invert in reverse order: $(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}$.

blocks.html: By now we have many ways to describe a square matrix: its inverse, its pivots, whether its columns are independent or span. For a square matrix, these are not separate facts. They all stand or fall together.
The Invertible Matrix Theorem. For an $n \times n$ matrix $A$, the following statements are equivalent (all true or all false):

items: (a) $A$ is invertible.
(b) $A$ is row equivalent to $I_n$.
(c) $A$ has $n$ pivot positions.
(d) $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ has only the trivial solution.
(e) The columns of $A$ are linearly independent.
(f) $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has at least one solution for every $\mathbf{b}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
(g) The columns of $A$ span $\mathbb{R}^n$.
(h) There is a matrix $C$ with $CA = I$; (i) there is a matrix $D$ with $AD = I$.
(j) $A^{T}$ is invertible.

blocks.html: The engine is counting pivots. A square matrix has $n$ rows and $n$ columns, so "a pivot in every column" and "a pivot in every row" both mean exactly $n$ pivots. A pivot in every column gives (d) and (e) (no free variables). A pivot in every row gives (f) and (g) (no row can become $0 = c$). And $n$ pivots in an $n \times n$ matrix means its RREF is $I$, which is (b), and then Gauss–Jordan produces the inverse, (a). Going back, if $A$ is invertible then $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ gives $\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}$. For a matrix that is not square, the row count and column count differ, and the statements split apart.

blocks.title: Using the theorem on a matrix
blocks.q: Is $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 & 7 \\ 1 & 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$ invertible? What does that say about its columns and about $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$?
steps: $R_2 \to R_2 - 2R_1$ and $R_3 \to R_3 - R_1$ give $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$, then $R_3 \to R_3 - 2R_2$: $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$.
Only 2 pivots for a $3 \times 3$ matrix, so (c) fails, and therefore every statement fails.
So $A$ is not invertible, its columns are dependent (indeed column 2 is twice column 1), they do not span $\mathbb{R}^3$, and some $\mathbf{b}$ make $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ inconsistent.
blocks.a: Not invertible; all the statements are false.

blocks.title: Reasoning without numbers
blocks.q: $A$ is $5 \times 5$, and $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has a solution for every $\mathbf{b}$ in $\mathbb{R}^5$. Can $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ have a nontrivial solution?
steps: The hypothesis is statement (f). Since $A$ is square, (f) implies all the others, including (d).
So $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ has only the trivial solution. (In fact, each $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has exactly one solution.)

blocks.name: matrix2d
blocks.cap: A singular $2 \times 2$ matrix: the unit square collapses to a segment (area 0). Its columns are dependent, many vectors land on the same point, and points off the line are never reached. Pick another preset to see an invertible one.

blocks.html: The theorem is for square matrices only. A $3 \times 4$ matrix can have columns that span $\mathbb{R}^3$ while its columns are dependent; a $4 \times 3$ matrix can have independent columns that do not span $\mathbb{R}^4$.

For a square matrix, invertible, $n$ pivots, independent columns, spanning columns, unique solutions and "only the trivial solution" are the same statement in different clothes. Check one, and you know them all.

blocks.html: Elimination, from echelon form, can be recorded as a factorization $A = LU$: $L$ is lower triangular and stores the multipliers, $U$ is the upper triangular echelon form. Computers solve most systems this way. The idea uses inverses of very simple matrices.

An elementary matrix is the identity with one row operation done to it. Multiplying $A$ on the left by an elementary matrix $E$ performs that same operation on $A$. For example, with $E = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, the product $EA$ is $A$ with $R_2 \to R_2 - 2R_1$. Each $E$ is invertible, and $E^{-1}$ is the opposite operation (here, put $+2$ in the same spot).

Why does $L$ just hold the multipliers? If elimination uses only replacements of a lower row by a multiple of a higher one, then $E_k \cdots E_2E_1A = U$, so $A = E_1^{-1}E_2^{-1}\cdots E_k^{-1}U$. Each $E_i^{-1}$ is lower triangular with one entry below the diagonal, and when you multiply them in this order the entries simply drop into place without interfering. So $L$ has $1$s on the diagonal and, in position $(i, j)$, the multiplier $\ell_{ij}$ that was subtracted: $R_i \to R_i - \ell_{ij}R_j$.

blocks.title: Finding L and U
blocks.q: Factor $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 4 & -1 & 3 \\ -2 & 5 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ as $LU$.
steps: $R_{3} \to R_{3} + 2R_{2}$ (multiplier $\ell_{32} = -2$, since we subtracted $-2$ times row 2): $U = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$.

blocks.name: la-rowops

opts.task: Press "Next step for me" three times and note each multiplier. They are the entries of $L$.

blocks.cap: Elimination on $A$ without swaps. The log lists the multipliers; the final matrix is $U$.

blocks.html: To solve $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$, write it as $L(U\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{b}$ and solve two triangular systems: first $L\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{b}$ from the top down, then $U\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{y}$ from the bottom up. When many right-hand sides share the same $A$ (common in engineering), the elimination is done once and each new $\mathbf{b}$ costs only the two quick triangular solves.

blocks.title: Two triangular solves
blocks.q: Use the factorization above to solve $A\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 11 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix}$.
steps: $L\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{b}$, top down: $y_1 = 3$; then $2y_1 + y_2 = 11$ gives $y_2 = 5$; then $-y_1 - 2y_2 + y_3 = -3$ gives $y_3 = -3 + 3 + 10 = 10$.
$U\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{y}$, bottom up: $5x_3 = 10$ gives $x_3 = 2$; $-3x_2 + x_3 = 5$ gives $x_2 = -1$; $2x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 3$ gives $x_1 = 1$.
Check in the original second equation: $4(1) - (-1) + 3(2) = 11$. ✓

Elimination without swaps is the factorization $A = LU$: $U$ is the echelon form and $L$ is unit lower triangular, holding the multipliers. Solve $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ by $L\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{b}$, then $U\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{y}$.

blocks.html: Multiplying by a matrix turns vectors into vectors: $\mathbf{x} \mapsto A\mathbf{x}$. In the matrix equation we saw that this respects sums and multiples. Now we turn that property into a definition and study the maps themselves.

A transformation (function, map) $T: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ assigns to each $\mathbf{x}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ (the domain) a vector $T(\mathbf{x})$ in $\mathbb{R}^m$ (the codomain). $T$ is linear if, for all vectors $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}$ and scalars $c$, $$T(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) = T(\mathbf{u}) + T(\mathbf{v}) \quad \text{and} \quad T(c\mathbf{u}) = cT(\mathbf{u}).$$ Every matrix map $T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$ is linear.

Two consequences follow straight from the definition. First, $T(\mathbf{0}) = \mathbf{0}$: since $\mathbf{0} = 0\cdot\mathbf{0}$, we get $T(\mathbf{0})$ $= T(0\cdot\mathbf{0})$ $= 0\cdot T(\mathbf{0})$ $= \mathbf{0}$. Second, superposition: $T(c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \cdots + c_p\mathbf{v}_p)$ $= c_1T(\mathbf{v}_1) + \cdots + c_pT(\mathbf{v}_p)$. So a linear map is completely known once you know what it does to a few vectors that build everything else.

blocks.title: Using linearity
blocks.q: $T$ is linear, $T(\mathbf{u}) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}$ and $T(\mathbf{v}) = \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$. Find $T(3\mathbf{u} - 2\mathbf{v})$.

blocks.title: Testing three maps
blocks.q: Which are linear? (a) $T(x, y) = (x + 2y,\ 3x)$; (b) $S(x, y) = (x + 1,\ y)$; (c) $R(x, y) = (xy,\ x)$.
steps: (a) Each output is a fixed combination of $x$ and $y$ with no constant, so $T(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\mathbf{x}$: linear.
(b) $S(0, 0) = (1, 0) \neq (0, 0)$. A linear map must fix the origin, so $S$ is not linear.
(c) $R(0, 0) = (0, 0)$, so test scaling: $R(2, 2) = (4, 2)$, but $2R(1, 1) = (2, 2)$. Not equal, so $R$ is not linear.

blocks.html: Calling a translation like $S(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}$ (with $\mathbf{b} \neq \mathbf{0}$) linear. It moves every point the same way and looks harmless, but it moves the origin: $S(\mathbf{0}) = \mathbf{b}$. Quick check for any formula: plug in $\mathbf{0}$ first. If you do not get $\mathbf{0}$, the map is not linear. (If you do get $\mathbf{0}$, you still need to check sums and multiples, as in (c).)

The set of all outputs $T(\mathbf{x})$ is the range of $T$. For $T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$, the range is the span of the columns of $A$. The range can be smaller than the codomain: the map $T(x, y) = (x + y, 2x + 2y)$ goes from $\mathbb{R}^2$ to $\mathbb{R}^2$, but every output lies on the line where the second entry is twice the first.

Why the name? A linear map sends lines to lines (or squashes them to a point): the line $\mathbf{p} + t\mathbf{v}$ goes to $T(\mathbf{p}) + tT(\mathbf{v})$, which is again a line, or a single point if $T(\mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{0}$. Equally spaced points along a line stay equally spaced. That is the "evenly spaced grid" you see in the picture.

Linear maps are everywhere: rotating a picture, converting currencies, mixing ingredients in fixed proportions, and the "linear approximation" of a smooth function in calculus, which is a linear map plus a constant.

A map is linear when it respects sums and scalar multiples. Then it sends $\mathbf{0}$ to $\mathbf{0}$ and turns combinations into the same combinations of the outputs. Matrix maps $\mathbf{x} \mapsto A\mathbf{x}$ are linear; translations are not.

blocks.html: Every matrix gives a linear transformation. The surprise is the converse: every linear transformation from $\mathbb{R}^n$ to $\mathbb{R}^m$ is multiplication by some matrix, and that matrix is easy to find.

If $T: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is linear, then $T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$ for the $m \times n$ standard matrix $$A = \left[\,T(\mathbf{e}_1)\ \ T(\mathbf{e}_2)\ \ \cdots\ \ T(\mathbf{e}_n)\,\right],$$ whose columns are the images of the standard basis vectors.

Any $\mathbf{x}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is $x_1\mathbf{e}_1 + x_2\mathbf{e}_2 + \cdots + x_n\mathbf{e}_n$. By linearity, $T(\mathbf{x})$ $= x_1T(\mathbf{e}_1) + \cdots + x_nT(\mathbf{e}_n)$. That is exactly the combination of the vectors $T(\mathbf{e}_j)$ with weights $x_j$, which by definition is $A\mathbf{x}$ for the matrix with those columns. So knowing $T$ on $n$ vectors tells you $T$ everywhere.

blocks.title: From a formula
blocks.q: Find the standard matrix of $T(x_1, x_2)$ $= (2x_1 - x_2,\ x_1 + 3x_2,\ -x_2)$.
steps: Use them as columns: $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$, a $3 \times 2$ matrix (from $\mathbb{R}^2$ to $\mathbb{R}^3$).

blocks.title: From the images of other vectors
blocks.q: $T$ is linear with $T\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $T\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$. Find its standard matrix.
steps: Write $\mathbf{e}_1$ and $\mathbf{e}_2$ using $\mathbf{u} = (1, 1)$ and $\mathbf{v} = (1, 2)$: $\mathbf{e}_1 = 2\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{e}_2 = \mathbf{v} - \mathbf{u}$. (Check: $2(1,1) - (1,2) = (1, 0)$ and $(1,2) - (1,1) = (0, 1)$.)

blocks.title: A map described in words
blocks.q: $T: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ rotates every vector $90^\circ$ about the $z$-axis (counterclockwise when seen from above). Find its standard matrix.
steps: $\mathbf{e}_1 = (1, 0, 0)$ turns to $(0, 1, 0)$; $\mathbf{e}_2 = (0, 1, 0)$ turns to $(-1, 0, 0)$; $\mathbf{e}_3 = (0, 0, 1)$ lies on the axis and stays put.
Check: $A\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ 2 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}$: the height $5$ is unchanged and $(2, 3)$ turned to $(-3, 2)$.

blocks.html: The size of the standard matrix is set by the map: $T: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ has $n$ columns (one per input direction $\mathbf{e}_j$) and $m$ rows (one per output entry). A formula like $T(x_1, x_2) = (\ldots, \ldots, \ldots)$ with three outputs always gives a $3 \times 2$ matrix.

blocks.html: Writing the images as rows instead of columns. With $T(\mathbf{e}_1) = (2, 1, 0)$ and $T(\mathbf{e}_2) = (-1, 3, -1)$, the matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$ is $2 \times 3$ and maps $\mathbb{R}^3$ to $\mathbb{R}^2$: the wrong direction. Check: multiply your matrix by $\mathbf{e}_1$; you must get $T(\mathbf{e}_1)$ back.

Why "standard"? The matrix records $T$ using the standard basis $\mathbf{e}_1, \dots, \mathbf{e}_n$ to describe inputs and outputs. Later, in change of basis, we will describe the same map using other, better-suited directions and get a different (often much simpler) matrix for the same $T$.

This is why we think of matrices and linear maps as two descriptions of the same thing. Questions about $T$ (Is it one-to-one? What is its range?) become questions about $A$ (pivots, columns), and row reduction answers them.

blocks.html: In precalculus you saw matrices move shapes. With the standard matrix rule ("columns are where $\mathbf{e}_1$ and $\mathbf{e}_2$ go"), you can build the matrix of any linear map of the plane yourself instead of memorizing a table.

Rotating $\mathbf{e}_1 = (1, 0)$ counterclockwise by $\theta$ lands on $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$, the point on the unit circle. Rotating $\mathbf{e}_2 = (0, 1)$, which starts a quarter-turn ahead, lands on $(\cos(\theta + 90^\circ), \sin(\theta + 90^\circ))$ $= (-\sin\theta, \cos\theta)$. So $$R_\theta = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}.$$

blocks.html: Why do all these maps have matrices at all? Each one is linear: rotating, reflecting, shearing or projecting a sum of arrows gives the sum of the rotated (reflected, …) arrows, because the parallelogram that builds the sum is carried along as a whole. Linear maps are determined by $T(\mathbf{e}_1)$ and $T(\mathbf{e}_2)$, so two pictures are all you need.

Each family has a fingerprint you can check. Rotations and reflections keep lengths and angles: their columns are perpendicular unit vectors. Rotations keep the F reading the same way; reflections flip it. A projection does nothing new the second time ($P^{2} = P$), and a shear keeps one direction fixed while sliding the other.

blocks.title: Reading a matrix
blocks.q: What does $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ do to the plane?
steps: The vector $(1, -1)$ stays put and $(1, 1)$ goes to $(-1, -1)$: the line $y = -x$ is fixed and the perpendicular direction flips.

blocks.html: To find the matrix of a plane map, ask where $\mathbf{e}_1$ and $\mathbf{e}_2$ go and use those as columns. Rotation by $\theta$: $\begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}$.

blocks.html: Doing one plane map after another gives a new map. This is where matrix multiplication comes from, and it explains why the order of a product matters.
If $T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$ and $S(\mathbf{x}) = B\mathbf{x}$, the composition $S \circ T$ means "first $T$, then $S$": $(S \circ T)(\mathbf{x}) = S(T(\mathbf{x}))$.
"First $T$ (matrix $A$), then $S$ (matrix $B$)" has standard matrix $BA$. The first map is written on the right, next to $\mathbf{x}$.

$S(T(\mathbf{x})) = B(A\mathbf{x}) = (BA)\mathbf{x}$, by the associative law, which is exactly what matrix multiplication was built to satisfy. Read a product right to left, the way the vector travels: in $BA\mathbf{x}$, the vector meets $A$ first.

steps: Check with $\mathbf{e}_1$: rotating gives $(0, 1)$; reflecting that gives $(0, -1)$, which is column 1 of $BA$. ✓
The result is the reflection across $y = -x$.

blocks.title: Angle addition from matrices
blocks.q: Show that rotating by $\alpha$ and then by $\beta$ is rotating by $\alpha + \beta$, and see what that says about cosines.
steps: The top-left entry is $\cos\beta\cos\alpha - \sin\beta\sin\alpha$, and the bottom-left is $\sin\beta\cos\alpha + \cos\beta\sin\alpha$.
Geometrically the product is $R_{\alpha + \beta}$, whose first column is $(\cos(\alpha + \beta), \sin(\alpha + \beta))$. Matching entries gives the angle addition formulas.

blocks.html: Multiplying in the order the maps are applied, getting $AB$ for "first $A$, then $B$". Check with one vector: apply the maps to $\mathbf{e}_1$ by hand, one at a time, and compare with column 1 of your product.

The same rule works for longer chains and for maps between different spaces. "First $A$, then $B$, then $C$" is $CBA$. If $T: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ and $S: \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^p$, then $A$ is $m \times n$, $B$ is $p \times m$, and $BA$ is $p \times n$: the sizes match exactly because the output space of $T$ is the input space of $S$. To undo a chain, undo the last step first: $(BA)^{-1} = A^{-1}B^{-1}$.
Rotations about the origin commute with each other ($R_\alpha R_\beta = R_\beta R_\alpha$), but rotations and reflections generally do not.

blocks.html: Two natural questions about a linear map $T: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$: does it ever send two different inputs to the same output, and does it reach every vector in $\mathbb{R}^m$? Both answers come from the pivots, just like existence and uniqueness for systems.
$T$ is one-to-one if each $\mathbf{b}$ in $\mathbb{R}^m$ is the image of at most one $\mathbf{x}$. $T$ is onto $\mathbb{R}^m$ if each $\mathbf{b}$ is the image of at least one $\mathbf{x}$.

For $T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$: $T$ is one-to-one exactly when $A$ has a pivot in every column (the columns are independent); $T$ is onto exactly when $A$ has a pivot in every row (the columns span $\mathbb{R}^m$).

One-to-one needs only one check: $T(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0}$ has only the solution $\mathbf{0}$. Indeed, if $T(\mathbf{u}) = T(\mathbf{v})$, then by linearity $T(\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{0}$; if only $\mathbf{0}$ maps to $\mathbf{0}$, then $\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$, so $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{v}$. And "only the trivial solution" means no free variables: a pivot in every column. Onto means $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ is consistent for every $\mathbf{b}$, which (from span) means a pivot in every row.

blocks.title: A map into a bigger space
blocks.q: $T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$ with $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$. Is $T$ one-to-one? Onto $\mathbb{R}^3$?
steps: Row reduce: $R_3 \to R_3 - 2R_1$ gives $(0, -1)$; $R_3 \to R_3 + R_2$ gives $(0, 0)$. Echelon form: $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$.
Row 3 has no pivot: not onto. The range is a plane in $\mathbb{R}^3$ (spanned by the two columns).

blocks.title: A map into a smaller space
steps: Standard matrix: $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$, already in echelon form.
Column 3 has no pivot: not one-to-one. For example, $T(1, -2, 1)$ $= (0, 0)$ $= T(0, 0, 0)$.

blocks.html: A practical way to think about it: a one-to-one map loses no information, since you can always tell which input produced an output. An onto map leaves nothing out, since every possible output really occurs. A map from a smaller space into a bigger one can be one-to-one but never onto; a map from a bigger space onto a smaller one can be onto but never one-to-one, because it must merge some inputs.
For a square matrix the two properties come together: by the Invertible Matrix Theorem, $T$ is one-to-one exactly when it is onto, exactly when $A$ is invertible.

blocks.html: A neural network sounds exotic, but you already know every part of it: matrix-vector products, ramps and composition. Networks built this way, with many more units and with weights found by training, are the math inside modern speech and image recognition and language models. Here is the whole idea at a size you can trace by hand.

A layer takes a vector $\mathbf{x}$, computes $\mathbf{z} = W\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}$, then applies ReLU to each entry: $\mathbf{h} = \operatorname{ReLU}(W\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b})$. Each hidden unit is a switch: on when its $z$ is positive (it passes $z$ through), off when $z \le 0$ (it outputs $0$). A two-layer network with one output computes $$y = \mathbf{v} \cdot \operatorname{ReLU}(W\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}) + c.$$

Why the switches matter: without them, $$\mathbf{v} \cdot (W\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}) + c = (\mathbf{v}^{T}W)\,\mathbf{x} + (\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{b} + c),$$ a single affine map, which is just a line or a plane. A composition of affine maps is affine, so stacking any number of switch-free layers never makes anything new. The ReLU between the layers breaks this. With one input, hidden unit $j$ adds the ramp $v_{j}\operatorname{ReLU}(w_{j}x + b_{j})$, which bends at $x = -b_{j}/w_{j}$, so the output is a sum of ramps: a bent-line graph with at most one bend per unit.

blocks.title: A forward pass by hand
blocks.q: Let $W = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{v} = (2, 5)$ and $c = -1$. Find $y$ for $\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}$.
steps: Output: $y = 2 \cdot 1 + 5 \cdot 0 - 1 = 1$. For this input the weight $5$ never mattered.

blocks.title: Turning a rule into weights
blocks.q: Build a network, with no training, that gives $10$ when $x \ge 5$ and $12$ otherwise, for every whole number $x$.
steps: A sum of ramps is continuous, so it cannot jump. But it can slide down by $2$ between $x = 4$ and $x = 5$, where there are no whole numbers to get wrong.
$\operatorname{ReLU}(x - 4) - \operatorname{ReLU}(x - 5)$ is $0$ for $x \le 4$, climbs to $1$ at $x = 5$, and then stays at $1$, because after $x = 5$ both ramps rise together.
Between $4$ and $5$ the output is a ramp: $x = 4.5$ gives $11$, a value the rule never gives. The network is exact on the inputs it was built for, the whole numbers, and only there.

blocks.html: This idea scales up. Handwired, a project by Cheng Lou, compiles ordinary if-else and loop code into fixed network weights built from affine maps and ReLU switches like these, with no training at all. The weights are exact for the inputs the program supports, and because they are ordinary weights, training could still adjust them later.

blocks.title: Logic with one switch
blocks.q: The inputs $x_{1}$ and $x_{2}$ are bits, $0$ or $1$. What does $y = x_{1} + x_{2} - 2\operatorname{ReLU}(x_{1} + x_{2} - 1)$ compute?
steps: The ramp $\operatorname{ReLU}(x_{1} + x_{2} - 1)$ is $1$ when both bits are $1$, and $0$ otherwise.

That is XOR: $1$ when exactly one bit is $1$. No affine map $px_{1} + qx_{2} + r$ can do this, because its values always satisfy $y(0, 0) + y(1, 1) = y(0, 1) + y(1, 0)$, while XOR has $0 + 0 \ne 1 + 1$. The switch is what makes it possible.

blocks.html: Switching before adding the bias. $\operatorname{ReLU}(W\mathbf{x}) + \mathbf{b}$ is not a layer. The bias goes in first, because it decides where each switch flips. In the first example, $\operatorname{ReLU}(W\mathbf{x}) + \mathbf{b} = (1, 1)$, but the layer gives $(1, 0)$. Check: every hidden output should be $0$ or positive.

Expecting more layers to help without switches. Two layers with no ReLU collapse into one affine map, as the box above shows. Check: if your network has no switches, multiply it out; you will get one matrix and one bias.

The output layer usually has no switch, so $y$ can be negative. Training means choosing $W$, $\mathbf{b}$, $\mathbf{v}$ and $c$ to fit examples. It uses gradient descent, with the derivatives found by backpropagation. The picture below does it on a small data set.

blocks.html: In precalculus you computed $2 \times 2$ and $3 \times 3$ determinants. The determinant is a single number that tells whether a square matrix is invertible (it is exactly when $\det A \neq 0$), and, as we will see, how much the matrix stretches area or volume. Cofactor expansion computes it for any size by breaking it into smaller determinants.

For a $2 \times 2$ matrix, $\det\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} = ad - bc$. For a larger $A$, let $A_{ij}$ be the matrix left after deleting row $i$ and column $j$. Its determinant $M_{ij} = \det A_{ij}$ is the minor, and $C_{ij} = (-1)^{i+j}M_{ij}$ is the cofactor.

For any row $i$: $\det A$ $= a_{i1}C_{i1} + a_{i2}C_{i2} + \cdots + a_{in}C_{in}$. For any column $j$: $\det A = a_{1j}C_{1j} + \cdots + a_{nj}C_{nj}$. Every row and every column gives the same answer, so expand along the one with the most zeros.
The signs $(-1)^{i+j}$ form a checkerboard that starts with $+$ in the top-left corner: $$\begin{bmatrix} + & - & + & - \\ - & + & - & + \\ + & - & + & - \\ - & + & - & + \end{bmatrix}$$

Where do the signs come from? The determinant changes sign when two rows (or two columns) are swapped. To bring entry $(i, j)$ to the top-left corner without disturbing the order of the other rows and columns, slide row $i$ up past $i - 1$ rows and column $j$ left past $j - 1$ columns: $(i - 1) + (j - 1)$ swaps in all, each flipping the sign. That is the factor $(-1)^{i+j}$. Expanding along the first row of the moved matrix gives $a_{ij}$ times the determinant of what is left, $M_{ij}$.

steps: Row 2 has a zero, so expand along it. Its signs are $-\ +\ -$.

steps: Row 3 has only one nonzero entry, $b_{33} = 5$, with sign $(-1)^{3+3} = +$.

blocks.html: Forgetting the checkerboard: adding every term with a $+$ sign. Only the positions where $i + j$ is even get $+$. Quick check: expand along a different row or column; if the two answers differ, a sign is wrong.
A useful special case: if $A$ is triangular (all zeros below or above the diagonal), expanding down the first column again and again shows that $\det A$ is the product of the diagonal entries.

blocks.html: Cofactor expansion is slow for big matrices. Row reduction from echelon form is fast, and the determinant changes in a simple, predictable way under each row operation.

head: Row operation
Effect on the determinant
rows: Replacement: add a multiple of one row to another
blocks.cap: How row operations change det A.

blocks.html: Two facts about the determinant do the work: it is linear in each row (if you fix the other rows, it is a linear function of the remaining one) and it changes sign when two rows are swapped. Scaling a row by $k$ multiplies by $k$ by linearity. A matrix with two equal rows has determinant $0$, because swapping those rows changes nothing yet must flip the sign. Then replacement: $$\det(\ldots, \mathbf{r}_i + c\mathbf{r}_j, \ldots) = \det(\ldots, \mathbf{r}_i, \ldots) + c\det(\ldots, \mathbf{r}_j, \ldots),$$ and the second determinant has row $\mathbf{r}_j$ twice, so it is $0$. Geometrically, a replacement is a shear, and shears do not change area.

blocks.title: Determinant by row reduction
blocks.q: Find $\det C$ for $C = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 1 & 3 & 5 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$.
steps: $R_{1} \leftrightarrow R_{2}$ to get a nonzero pivot: the determinant flips sign. $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$
$R_{3} \to R_{3} - 2R_{1}$ and then $R_{3} \to R_{3} + \frac{5}{2}R_{2}$ (replacements, no change): $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$

blocks.html: This gives a fast method for any size: row reduce to an echelon form $U$ using replacements and swaps only. If you made $r$ swaps, then $\det A$ is $(-1)^{r}$ times the product of the diagonal entries of $U$. For a $20 \times 20$ matrix that is a few thousand arithmetic steps instead of the $20!$ terms of cofactor expansion.

items: $\det(AB) = (\det A)(\det B)$.
$\det A^{T} = \det A$, so everything said about rows holds for columns too.
$A$ is invertible exactly when $\det A \neq 0$, and then $\det A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{\det A}$ (from $\det A \cdot \det A^{-1} = \det I = 1$).
For an $n \times n$ matrix, $\det(kA) = k^{n}\det A$: every one of the $n$ rows is scaled by $k$.

blocks.title: Combining the rules
blocks.q: $A$ and $B$ are $3 \times 3$ with $\det A = 2$ and $\det B = -5$. Find $\det(2A^{T}B^{-1})$.

blocks.html: Assuming $\det(A + B) = \det A + \det B$. The determinant respects products, not sums. With $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$: $\det A + \det B = -2 + 6 = 4$, but $A + B = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 4 & 7 \end{bmatrix}$ has determinant $21 - 8 = 13$. Quick check: try $A = B = I_2$; then $\det(2I) = 4$, not $2$.

blocks.html: Reduce to triangular form, multiply the diagonal, and correct for the operations: each swap flips the sign, each scaling by $k$ multiplies by $k$, replacements change nothing. And $\det(AB) = \det A\det B$, $\det A^{T} = \det A$, $\det A^{-1} = 1/\det A$.

blocks.html: The rules for determinants have a picture behind them. For a $2 \times 2$ matrix, $|\det A|$ is the area of the parallelogram spanned by its columns; for $3 \times 3$, the volume of the slanted box. And the map $\mathbf{x} \mapsto A\mathbf{x}$ multiplies every area (or volume) by that same factor.

$|\det A|$ is the factor by which $\mathbf{x} \mapsto A\mathbf{x}$ scales area (in $\mathbb{R}^2$) or volume (in $\mathbb{R}^3$). The sign of $\det A$ says whether the map keeps or reverses orientation.

blocks.name: matrix2d

opts.task: Press "Apply A" and compare the gold area with det A. Then try the "Reflect" preset.

blocks.cap: The unit square (area 1) becomes the parallelogram spanned by the columns, with area $|\det A|$. A red parallelogram means the map flipped the plane.

blocks.html: Why area? The unit square has area $1$ and goes to the parallelogram spanned by the columns. Now follow the row-operation rules geometrically. A shear (replacement) slides the parallelogram along a side without changing its base or height, so the area stays; scaling a side by $k$ scales the area by $|k|$; and a triangular (or diagonal) matrix gives a parallelogram with base $|a_{11}|$ and height $|a_{22}|$. These match the rules for $\det$ step by step, so $|\det A|$ and the area must agree. Any other region is (nearly) a union of tiny grid squares, each scaled by the same factor, so every area scales by $|\det A|$.

blocks.title: Area of a parallelogram
blocks.q: Find the area of the parallelogram with sides $\mathbf{u} = (3, 1)$ and $\mathbf{v} = (1, 2)$.

blocks.title: Area of a triangle
blocks.q: Find the area of the triangle with vertices $(1, 1)$, $(4, 2)$ and $(2, 5)$.
steps: Move one vertex to the origin. Edge vectors from $(1, 1)$: $\mathbf{a} = (3, 1)$ and $\mathbf{b} = (1, 4)$.
They span a parallelogram of area $\left|\det\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\right|$ $= |12 - 1|$ $= 11$.
The triangle is half of it: $\frac{11}{2}$.

blocks.title: The image of a disk
blocks.q: $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$ maps the unit disk to an ellipse. What is the ellipse's area?
steps: $\det A = 6$, so every area is multiplied by $6$.
The unit disk has area $\pi$, so the ellipse has area $6\pi$.

blocks.title: Volume of a parallelepiped
blocks.q: Find the volume of the box with edges $(1, 2, 0)$, $(0, 1, 3)$ and $(2, 0, 1)$.
steps: Put the edges in the columns: $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.

blocks.html: A negative determinant means the map is orientation-reversing: it turns counterclockwise order into clockwise, like a mirror. A zero determinant means the map squashes the plane onto a line (or a point), so all areas become $0$, and the matrix cannot be invertible.
Reporting a negative area. Area and volume are $|\det A|$; the sign is extra information about orientation. Also remember the triangle is half the parallelogram.

blocks.html: Determinants give a formula for each unknown of a square system and for each entry of an inverse. These formulas are rarely the fastest way to compute, but they show exactly how the answer depends on the data, which matters in theory and in hand calculations with symbols.
For an $n \times n$ invertible $A$ and a vector $\mathbf{b}$, let $A_i(\mathbf{b})$ be $A$ with column $i$ replaced by $\mathbf{b}$.

Cramer's rule. The unique solution of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has $x_i = \dfrac{\det A_i(\mathbf{b})}{\det A}$. Adjugate formula. $A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{\det A}\operatorname{adj} A$, where $\operatorname{adj} A$ is the transpose of the matrix of cofactors: its $(i, j)$ entry is $C_{ji}$.

Let $I_i(\mathbf{x})$ be the identity with column $i$ replaced by $\mathbf{x}$. Expanding along row $i$ shows $\det I_i(\mathbf{x}) = x_i$. Now $A\,I_i(\mathbf{x})$ has columns $A\mathbf{e}_1, \dots, A\mathbf{x}, \dots, A\mathbf{e}_n$, which are the columns of $A$ except that column $i$ is $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$. So $A\,I_i(\mathbf{x}) = A_i(\mathbf{b})$. Take determinants with the product rule: $\det A \cdot x_i = \det A_i(\mathbf{b})$. Divide by $\det A$. Applying this to $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{e}_j$ (column $j$ of $A^{-1}$) gives the adjugate formula.

blocks.title: One entry of an inverse
blocks.q: For $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, find the entry of $A^{-1}$ in row 1, column 3.
steps: Entry $(1, 3)$ of $\operatorname{adj} A$ is the cofactor $C_{31}$ (indices swapped): $C_{31} = (+1)\begin{vmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = 6$.

blocks.html: For a $2 \times 2$ matrix the adjugate is the familiar swap-and-negate: $\operatorname{adj}\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}$ $= \begin{bmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{bmatrix}$, which is where the $2 \times 2$ inverse formula comes from.
Using $C_{ij}$ instead of $C_{ji}$ in position $(i, j)$: the adjugate is the transpose of the cofactor matrix. Check: multiply $A$ by your adjugate; you should get $(\det A)I$.

blocks.name: linesystem
blocks.cap: The system from the first example: the lines cross at $(2, 1)$, the point Cramer's rule found.

blocks.html: Cramer's rule also explains how sensitive a solution can be. Every unknown is a ratio with $\det A$ in the denominator. When $\det A$ is tiny compared with the entries, small changes in $\mathbf{b}$ can cause big swings in $\mathbf{x}$: in the picture, the two lines are nearly parallel, and nudging one of them slides the crossing point far along the other.

For an $n \times n$ system, Cramer's rule needs $n + 1$ determinants. Row reduction is far cheaper for anything beyond small systems, so use Cramer for theory, $2 \times 2$ cases and systems with letters in them. One theoretical payoff: every entry of $A^{-1}$ is a polynomial in the entries of $A$ divided by $\det A$, so the inverse changes smoothly as long as $\det A$ stays away from $0$.

blocks.html: So far we have mostly computed. From here on, many statements are about all matrices or all vectors of some kind, and we need a way to be sure of them. That way is a proof: a chain of small steps, each justified by a definition, the hypothesis, or a fact proved earlier. You met the logic of "if $P$, then $Q$" in geometry; here it meets linear independence and its friends.

Why can't examples prove a general claim? A statement like "for all $n \times n$ matrices $A$ and $B$, $(AB)^{T} = B^{T}A^{T}$" covers infinitely many cases, and checking ten of them leaves infinitely many unchecked. A proof instead works with an arbitrary object: it names one that satisfies the hypothesis and uses only what every such object must satisfy. The other direction is easier: a single counterexample is enough to show a "for all" claim is false.

blocks.text: The shape of a direct proof

items: Write down what you are given, for arbitrary objects: "Let $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ be vectors with $A\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}$ and $A\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$."
Write down what you must show, in terms of definitions: "We must show $A(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{0}$."
Connect the two with small steps, each with a reason.

blocks.title: A direct proof
blocks.q: Prove: if $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are solutions of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$, then so is $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}$.
steps: Let $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ be any vectors with $A\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}$ and $A\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$.
$A(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) = A\mathbf{u} + A\mathbf{v}$, because matrix-vector multiplication distributes over addition.
blocks.a: Proved for every pair of solutions, not just one example.

blocks.title: Disproving with a counterexample
blocks.q: True or false: if $AB = 0$ (the zero matrix), then $A = 0$ or $B = 0$.
steps: Try simple matrices with many zeros. Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.
$AB = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, yet neither $A$ nor $B$ is the zero matrix.
One counterexample is enough: the statement is false. (For numbers, $ab = 0$ forces $a = 0$ or $b = 0$; matrices are different.)

blocks.title: Proof by contrapositive
blocks.q: Prove: if $\{\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3\}$ is linearly independent, then $\{\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2\}$ is linearly independent.
steps: The contrapositive of "if $P$, then $Q$" is "if not $Q$, then not $P$", and it is true exactly when the original is. Here: if $\{\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2\}$ is dependent, then $\{\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3\}$ is dependent.
Suppose $\{\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2\}$ is dependent: $c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + c_2\mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{0}$ with $c_1, c_2$ not both $0$.
Then $c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + c_2\mathbf{v}_2 + 0\mathbf{v}_3 = \mathbf{0}$, and the weights are still not all $0$.
That is a dependence relation for the three vectors, so they are dependent. $\blacksquare$
blocks.a: Every subset of an independent set is independent.

blocks.html: Checking one example (or five) and calling it a proof. Examples are excellent for guessing what is true and for finding counterexamples, but they cannot show a "for all" statement. Quick test of your argument: does any step use a specific number from your example? If so, it is not yet a proof.

A related trap is proving the converse by accident. "If $A$ is invertible, then $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ has only the trivial solution" is a different statement from "if $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ has only the trivial solution, then $A$ is invertible" (the second needs $A$ to be square). Keep track of which way the arrow points.

blocks.html: A proof handles an arbitrary case using definitions and earlier results, one justified step at a time. Examples suggest, a counterexample refutes, and only a proof establishes a statement about all cases.
