blocks.html: Everything we have done with vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ used only a few rules: you can add, you can scale, and the usual algebra holds. Many other objects follow the same rules, so the same ideas apply to them. With the tools of short proofs and span, we can now say this precisely.

A vector space is a set $V$ with an addition and a scalar multiplication such that sums and multiples stay in $V$ and the familiar rules hold: $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{u}$, $(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) + \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{u} + (\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w})$, there is a zero vector with $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{u}$, each $\mathbf{u}$ has a negative, $c(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) = c\mathbf{u} + c\mathbf{v}$, $(c + d)\mathbf{u} = c\mathbf{u} + d\mathbf{u}$, $c(d\mathbf{u}) = (cd)\mathbf{u}$ and $1\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{u}$. Examples: $\mathbb{R}^n$; the polynomials $\mathbb{P}_n$ of degree at most $n$; all $m \times n$ matrices; all functions on an interval.
A subspace $H$ of $V$ is a subset that is a vector space on its own, using the same operations. Most of the rules are inherited, so only three things need checking:

items: (1) $\mathbf{0}$ is in $H$;
(2) $H$ is closed under addition: if $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}$ are in $H$, so is $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}$;
(3) $H$ is closed under scalar multiplication: if $\mathbf{u}$ is in $H$, so is $c\mathbf{u}$ for every $c$.

blocks.html: A subspace contains $\mathbf{0}$ and is closed under addition and scaling. Every span is a subspace, and in $\mathbb{R}^3$ the subspaces are exactly: $\{\mathbf{0}\}$, lines through the origin, planes through the origin, and $\mathbb{R}^3$ itself.

Why is a span always a subspace? $\mathbf{0} = 0\mathbf{v}_1 + \cdots + 0\mathbf{v}_p$ is in it. The sum of two combinations, $(a_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \cdots) + (b_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \cdots)$ $= (a_1 + b_1)\mathbf{v}_1 + \cdots$, is again a combination, and so is $c(a_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \cdots)$ $= (ca_1)\mathbf{v}_1 + \cdots$. Lines and planes that miss the origin fail test (1), so they are never subspaces.

blocks.name: span
blocks.cap: The plane $x - 2y + z = 0$ is the span of $(2, 1, 0)$ and $(-1, 0, 1)$: a subspace. Every combination stays in the plane.

blocks.title: A plane through the origin
blocks.q: Show that $H = \{(x, y, z) : x - 2y + z = 0\}$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3$.
steps: All three hold. (Or: $H$ is the null space of $[\,1\ \ -2\ \ 1\,]$, as the next topic will show.)

blocks.title: Two that fail
blocks.q: Are these subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^2$? (a) $\{(x, y) : x \geq 0\}$; (b) $\{(x, y) : y = x^{2}\}$.
steps: (a) Contains $\mathbf{0}$ and is closed under addition, but $(1, 0)$ is in it while $-1\cdot(1, 0) = (-1, 0)$ is not. Fails (3).
(b) Contains $(0, 0)$. But $(1, 1)$ is in it and $(1, 1) + (1, 1) = (2, 2)$ is not, since $2 \neq 2^{2}$. Fails (2).

blocks.title: Polynomials
blocks.q: Is $H = \{p \text{ in } \mathbb{P}_2 : p(2) = 0\}$ a subspace of $\mathbb{P}_2$?
steps: The zero polynomial has value $0$ at $2$.

blocks.html: Skipping the zero-vector check, or stopping after it. A set like $\{(x, y, z) : x - 2y + z = 5\}$ looks just like the plane above, but $\mathbf{0}$ is not in it, so it is not a subspace. And passing the zero test is not enough either, as the parabola in (b) shows. Check all three conditions, and to say "no", give one specific failure.

blocks.html: Every matrix comes with two important subspaces. One collects the inputs that $A$ sends to $\mathbf{0}$ (the solutions of a homogeneous system); the other collects all possible outputs.

For an $m \times n$ matrix $A$: the null space $\operatorname{Nul} A$ $= \{\mathbf{x} \text{ in } \mathbb{R}^n : A\mathbf{x}$ $= \mathbf{0}\}$, and the column space $\operatorname{Col} A$ = the span of the columns of $A$ = $\{A\mathbf{x}\}$, a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^m$.

$\operatorname{Nul} A$ is a subspace: $A\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}$; if $A\mathbf{u} = A\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$, then $A(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{0}$ and $A(c\mathbf{u}) = \mathbf{0}$. $\operatorname{Col} A$ is a span, so it is a subspace. Notice they live in different places: null space vectors have $n$ entries (inputs), column space vectors have $m$ entries (outputs).

head: Nul A
Col A
rows: a list: all combinations of the columns
blocks.cap: The two spaces side by side.

blocks.title: A basis for Nul A
blocks.q: Find vectors that span $\operatorname{Nul} A$ for $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & 4 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & -2 & 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$.
steps: Pivots in columns 1 and 3; $x_2 = s$ and $x_4 = t$ are free. Then $x_1 = -2s + t$ and $x_3 = -3t$.
These two are independent (look at entries 2 and 4), so they form a basis. Check: $A\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ -3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{0}$ ✓.
blocks.a: Two vectors, one per free variable.

blocks.title: A basis for Col A
blocks.q: Find a basis for $\operatorname{Col} A$ for the same $A$.
steps: The pivot columns are 1 and 3, so take columns 1 and 3 of $A$: $\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$.
The other columns depend on these: column 2 is $2\times$ column 1, and column 4 is $-(\text{column }1) + 3(\text{column }3)$, exactly as the reduced matrix says.

blocks.html: Why the pivot columns of $A$? Row operations do not change the solutions of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$, and those solutions are exactly the dependence relations among the columns. So the columns of $A$ satisfy the same relations as the columns of its reduced form $R$. In $R$ the pivot columns are clearly independent and every other column is a combination of them; therefore the same is true for the corresponding columns of $A$.

Taking the pivot columns of the reduced matrix as a basis for $\operatorname{Col} A$. Row operations keep the relations between columns but change the column space itself. Here $R$ has pivot columns $(1, 0, 0)$ and $(0, 1, 0)$, but $(1, 0, 0)$ is not even in $\operatorname{Col} A$. Use $R$ to locate the pivots, then copy the columns from $A$.

blocks.name: matrix2d
blocks.cap: For $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$, the line through $(2, -1)$ is sent to $\mathbf{0}$: that is $\operatorname{Nul} A$. Every output lands on the line through $(1, 2)$: that is $\operatorname{Col} A$.

blocks.html: $\operatorname{Nul} A$ (in $\mathbb{R}^n$) holds the solutions of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$; its basis comes from the free variables. $\operatorname{Col} A$ (in $\mathbb{R}^m$) is spanned by the columns; its basis is the pivot columns of the original $A$.

blocks.html: A spanning set might contain redundant vectors; an independent set might not reach everything. A basis is a set that does both jobs with nothing wasted. It combines spanning sets for subspaces with independence.
A basis of a subspace $H$ is a set of vectors in $H$ that is linearly independent and spans $H$. Then every vector in $H$ can be written as a combination of the basis vectors in exactly one way.

Why exactly one way? Spanning gives at least one. Suppose $\mathbf{x}$ $= c_1\mathbf{b}_1 + \cdots + c_p\mathbf{b}_p$ $= d_1\mathbf{b}_1 + \cdots + d_p\mathbf{b}_p$. Subtract: $(c_1 - d_1)\mathbf{b}_1 + \cdots + (c_p - d_p)\mathbf{b}_p$ $= \mathbf{0}$. Independence forces every $c_i - d_i = 0$, so the two ways were the same. Those unique weights are the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis.

items: The standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$: $\mathbf{e}_1, \dots, \mathbf{e}_n$.
$\{1, t, t^{2}\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{P}_2$: every polynomial $a + bt + ct^{2}$ is a unique combination.
Any $n$ independent vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ form a basis (by the Invertible Matrix Theorem, they also span).

opts.task: Reach the star. There is exactly one pair of weights that works.

blocks.cap: Two independent vectors are a basis of the plane. The dots are combinations with whole-number weights; every point is reached by exactly one pair of weights.

blocks.title: Not a basis
blocks.q: Is $\left\{\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\right\}$ a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$?
steps: Three vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$: they form a basis exactly when the matrix with these columns has 3 pivots (equivalently, nonzero determinant).

blocks.title: A basis for a plane
blocks.q: Find a basis for the plane $x + y - z = 0$.
steps: Solve for $x$: $x = -y + z$, with $y = s$ and $z = t$ free.
The two vectors span the plane and are not multiples of each other, so they are a basis.

blocks.html: Trimming a spanning set. If $H = \operatorname{Span}\{\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_p\}$ and some $\mathbf{v}_k$ is a combination of the others, removing it leaves the span unchanged (anything built with $\mathbf{v}_k$ can be rebuilt without it). Keep removing until the set is independent: what is left is a basis. With a matrix, this is just "keep the pivot columns".

Bases also exist in other vector spaces. In $\mathbb{P}_2$, the set $\{1, t, t^{2}\}$ works, and so does $\{1,\ 1 + t,\ (1 + t)^{2}\}$; the second is handy for describing polynomials near $t = -1$. Choosing a basis is choosing a coordinate system, which is the subject of change of basis.
A basis is a smallest spanning set and a largest independent set. Add any vector of $H$ to a basis and it becomes dependent; remove any vector and it stops spanning.

Calling a set a basis after checking only one condition. A spanning set can be dependent (too many vectors), and an independent set can fail to span (too few). For $n$ vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ one check is enough, but in general you need both.

blocks.html: A plane has many different bases, but every one of them has two vectors. That number, the same for every basis, measures the size of a subspace.

Every basis of a subspace $H$ has the same number of vectors, called the dimension of $H$, $\dim H$. The rank of a matrix is $\dim \operatorname{Col} A$, the number of pivot columns; $\dim \operatorname{Nul} A$ is the number of free variables.

Why can't one basis have 2 vectors and another 3? The key fact: if $p$ vectors span $H$, then any set of more than $p$ vectors in $H$ is dependent. Write each of the bigger set's vectors in terms of the $p$ spanning vectors; their weight vectors are more than $p$ vectors in $\mathbb{R}^p$, so they are dependent (more columns than rows), and the same dependence relation holds for the original vectors. So a basis (independent) can never be bigger than another basis (spanning), in either direction. They must be the same size.

blocks.title: Rank and nullity of a matrix
blocks.q: Find $\operatorname{rank} A$ and $\dim \operatorname{Nul} A$ for $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$.

blocks.title: Dimension of a span
blocks.q: Find the dimension of $$\operatorname{Span}\left\{\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}\right\}.$$
steps: These are the columns of the matrix in the first example, which has 2 pivots.
So the span is 2-dimensional: a plane in $\mathbb{R}^3$, with basis $\{(1, 0, 1), (2, 1, 3)\}$ (the pivot columns).

blocks.title: Dimension of a solution space
blocks.q: What is the dimension of the subspace of $\mathbb{R}^5$ given by $$x_1 - x_3 + 2x_5 = 0 \quad\text{and}\quad x_2 + x_4 = 0?$$
steps: It is the null space of $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, already in RREF.
Two pivots, five columns: three free variables, so dimension $3$.

blocks.html: For a subspace given as a span, the dimension is the rank of the matrix whose columns are the spanning vectors. For a subspace given by equations, it is the number of free variables. These are the two ways subspaces usually appear, and both reduce to counting pivots.

Two consequences you can use right away. In a $p$-dimensional space, any $p$ independent vectors automatically span (so they form a basis), and any $p$ vectors that span are automatically independent. And a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$ never has dimension bigger than $n$.

blocks.html: Rank counts pivot columns; nullity counts free columns. Together they account for every column, and that simple count connects the size of the outputs to the size of what gets lost. It sharpens what we learned about one-to-one and onto maps.
Rank–nullity theorem. For an $m \times n$ matrix $A$: $\operatorname{rank} A + \dim \operatorname{Nul} A = n$, the number of columns.

Every column of $A$ is either a pivot column or a free column, never both. The pivot columns give a basis of $\operatorname{Col} A$, so there are $\operatorname{rank} A$ of them. The free columns each give one vector in a basis of $\operatorname{Nul} A$, so there are $\dim \operatorname{Nul} A$ of them. The two counts add up to $n$. For a linear map $T: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ this reads: $\dim(\text{range}) + \dim(\text{kernel})$ $= n$. Every input dimension either shows up in the output or gets crushed to $\mathbf{0}$.

The row space $\operatorname{Row} A$ is the span of the rows of $A$ (a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$). Row operations replace rows by combinations of rows, so they never change the row space, and the nonzero rows of an echelon form are a basis. That gives $\dim \operatorname{Row} A = \operatorname{rank} A$: the row rank equals the column rank. Applying rank–nullity to $A^{T}$ as well gives four subspaces with linked sizes:

blocks.html: A basis lets us describe every vector by its weights. The standard basis is only one choice. Often another basis fits a problem better, and then we need to translate between descriptions. The translation uses inverse matrices.

If $\mathcal{B} = \{\mathbf{b}_1, \dots, \mathbf{b}_n\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\mathbf{x} = c_1\mathbf{b}_1 + \cdots + c_n\mathbf{b}_n$, the coordinate vector of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to $\mathcal{B}$ is $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}} = (c_1, \dots, c_n)$. With $P_{\mathcal{B}} = [\,\mathbf{b}_1\ \cdots\ \mathbf{b}_n\,]$, that equation says $$\mathbf{x} = P_{\mathcal{B}}[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}, \qquad [\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}} = P_{\mathcal{B}}^{-1}\mathbf{x}.$$

opts.task: Find the weights that reach the star: they are its coordinates in this basis.

blocks.cap: The grid of the basis $\mathbf{b}_1 = (2, 1)$, $\mathbf{b}_2 = (1, 1)$. The point $(5, 4)$ is $1$ step along $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $3$ steps along $\mathbf{b}_2$, so its $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates are $(1, 3)$.

blocks.title: Finding coordinates
blocks.q: With $\mathcal{B} = \left\{\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\right\}$, find $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ for $\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}$.

blocks.html: For two bases $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$, the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\mathcal{C} \leftarrow \mathcal{B}}$ turns $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates into $\mathcal{C}$-coordinates: $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{C}} = P_{\mathcal{C} \leftarrow \mathcal{B}}[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$. Its columns are the $\mathcal{C}$-coordinates of the $\mathcal{B}$ vectors, $P_{\mathcal{C} \leftarrow \mathcal{B}}$ $= \left[\,[\mathbf{b}_1]_{\mathcal{C}}\ \cdots\ [\mathbf{b}_n]_{\mathcal{C}}\,\right]$ $= P_{\mathcal{C}}^{-1}P_{\mathcal{B}}$, and going back uses its inverse.

Read $P_{\mathcal{C}}^{-1}P_{\mathcal{B}}$ right to left, the way a vector travels: $P_{\mathcal{B}}$ turns $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates into ordinary (standard) coordinates, and then $P_{\mathcal{C}}^{-1}$ turns ordinary coordinates into $\mathcal{C}$-coordinates. The column formula says the same thing: $\mathbf{b}_j$ has $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates $\mathbf{e}_j$, so column $j$ must be $[\mathbf{b}_j]_{\mathcal{C}}$.

blocks.title: A change-of-coordinates matrix
blocks.q: $\mathcal{B}$ is as above and $\mathcal{C} = \left\{\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\right\}$. Find $P_{\mathcal{C} \leftarrow \mathcal{B}}$.
steps: Use it on the earlier vector: $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{C}}$ $= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$ $= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}$, and indeed $1(1, 0) + 4(1, 1) = (5, 4)$.

blocks.html: Using the matrix in the wrong direction: multiplying $\mathbf{x}$ by $P_{\mathcal{B}}$ to "get $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates". $P_{\mathcal{B}}$ goes from $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates to standard ones; for the other direction you need $P_{\mathcal{B}}^{-1}$. Quick check: feed in $\mathbf{b}_1$. Its $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates must come out as $(1, 0, \dots, 0)$.

Why bother with other bases? A basis adapted to a problem makes it simpler. In a picture tilted at an angle, coordinates along the tilt are more natural; in a vibrating system, coordinates along the natural modes separate the motion; in data, coordinates along the main directions of spread compress the information. All of these are changes of basis.

Changing basis also changes the matrix of a map. If $T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$, then in $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates $T$ has matrix $P_{\mathcal{B}}^{-1}AP_{\mathcal{B}}$. Choosing a basis that makes this matrix diagonal is the whole idea behind diagonalization.

$[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}} = P_{\mathcal{B}}^{-1}\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{x} = P_{\mathcal{B}}[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$. Between bases, $P_{\mathcal{C} \leftarrow \mathcal{B}} = P_{\mathcal{C}}^{-1}P_{\mathcal{B}}$, whose columns are the $\mathcal{C}$-coordinates of the $\mathcal{B}$ vectors.

blocks.html: Apply a matrix to most vectors and they turn to point in a new direction. A few special vectors do not turn at all: the matrix only stretches them, shrinks them or flips them. Those directions reveal what the matrix really does, and finding them uses null spaces.

An eigenvector of an $n \times n$ matrix $A$ is a nonzero vector $\mathbf{v}$ with $$A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$$ for some number $\lambda$, called the eigenvalue for $\mathbf{v}$. The eigenvalue can be any number, including $0$ or a negative number (a flip).

blocks.name: matrix2d

opts.task: Drag $\mathbf{v}$ until $A\mathbf{v}$ points along the same line as $\mathbf{v}$. Find two different lines.

blocks.cap: The dashed purple lines are the eigenvector directions of $A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$: along them, $A$ only stretches (by 5 and by 2).

blocks.title: Checking candidates
blocks.q: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$. Are $\mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{w} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{z} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$ eigenvectors?
steps: $A\mathbf{z} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$, which is not a multiple of $(1, 0)$: not an eigenvector.

blocks.html: To find eigenvectors for a given $\lambda$, rewrite $A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$ as $A\mathbf{v} - \lambda I\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$, that is, $$(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}.$$ (We write $\lambda I\mathbf{v}$ rather than $\lambda\mathbf{v}$ so that both terms are matrices times $\mathbf{v}$.) So the eigenvectors for $\lambda$ are the nonzero vectors in $\operatorname{Nul}(A - \lambda I)$, and $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue exactly when that null space contains a nonzero vector: when $A - \lambda I$ is not invertible.

blocks.title: Finding eigenvectors for a given eigenvalue
blocks.q: Find the eigenvectors of $A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$ for $\lambda = 2$.
steps: Both rows say $2x_1 + x_2 = 0$, so $x_2 = -2x_1$ with $x_1$ free.

Eigenvectors: all nonzero multiples of $\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}$. Check: $A\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -4 \end{bmatrix} = 2\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}$. ✓

blocks.title: Is 3 an eigenvalue?
blocks.q: Is $\lambda = 3$ an eigenvalue of the same $A$?
steps: $A - 3I = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ has determinant $0 - 2 = -2 \neq 0$, so it is invertible.
Then $(A - 3I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ only for $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$, which does not count.

blocks.html: Accepting the zero vector as an eigenvector. $A\mathbf{0} = \lambda\mathbf{0}$ is true for every number $\lambda$, so allowing it would make every number an eigenvalue and the idea would mean nothing. Eigenvectors must be nonzero; eigenvalues may be $0$. (And $\lambda = 0$ is an eigenvalue exactly when $A\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ for some $\mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}$: when $A$ is not invertible.)

Any nonzero multiple of an eigenvector is again an eigenvector for the same eigenvalue, since $A(c\mathbf{v}) = cA\mathbf{v} = \lambda(c\mathbf{v})$. So we really find eigenvector directions, and when an answer needs one specific vector we fix a convenient entry, such as making the first entry $1$.

$A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$ with $\mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}$: along $\mathbf{v}$, $A$ just multiplies by $\lambda$. The eigenvectors for $\lambda$ are the nonzero solutions of $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$, and $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue exactly when $A - \lambda I$ is not invertible.

blocks.html: Eigenvalues are the numbers $\lambda$ that make $A - \lambda I$ singular. Determinants detect singularity, so they turn the search for eigenvalues into solving one polynomial equation.

$\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$ exactly when $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$, the characteristic equation. For an $n \times n$ matrix, $\det(A - \lambda I)$ is a polynomial of degree $n$ in $\lambda$, the characteristic polynomial.

By the Invertible Matrix Theorem, $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ has a nonzero solution exactly when $A - \lambda I$ is not invertible, exactly when its determinant is $0$. Each entry of $A - \lambda I$ is a number or a number minus $\lambda$, and a determinant is a sum of products of $n$ entries, so the result is a polynomial in $\lambda$ of degree $n$.

blocks.title: A 2 × 2 matrix
blocks.q: Find the eigenvalues of $A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$.
steps: Check: the eigenvalues add to $7 = 4 + 3$ (the trace) and multiply to $10 = \det A$.

blocks.html: For any $2 \times 2$ matrix the polynomial is $\lambda^{2} - (\operatorname{tr} A)\lambda + \det A$, where the trace $\operatorname{tr} A$ is the sum of the diagonal entries. In general, the eigenvalues (counted with multiplicity) add up to the trace and multiply to the determinant: a free check on your arithmetic.

blocks.title: A 3 × 3 matrix
blocks.q: Find the eigenvalues of $B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$.
steps: Expand $\det(B - \lambda I)$ along row 1, which has two zeros: $$(2 - \lambda)\begin{vmatrix} 3 - \lambda & -1 \\ 2 & -\lambda \end{vmatrix}.$$
Eigenvalues: $2$ (a double root) and $1$. Check: $2 + 2 + 1 = 5 = \operatorname{tr} B$ and $2 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 4 = \det B$.

blocks.html: The number of times a root repeats is its algebraic multiplicity; here $\lambda = 2$ has multiplicity 2. For a triangular matrix, $A - \lambda I$ is triangular too, so its determinant is the product of the diagonal entries: the eigenvalues of a triangular matrix are its diagonal entries.

Subtracting $\lambda$ from every entry instead of only the diagonal. $\lambda I$ has $\lambda$ on the diagonal and $0$ elsewhere, so the off-diagonal entries of $A - \lambda I$ are the same as those of $A$. Quick check: the eigenvalues should add up to the trace.

blocks.cap: This is $A - 5I$ for the first example. Its determinant is $0$: it squashes the plane onto a line, so some nonzero vector (an eigenvector of $A$) is sent to $\mathbf{0}$.

blocks.html: A real polynomial can have complex roots, so a real matrix can have complex eigenvalues (a rotation, for example). We return to these in complex eigenvalues. Also, row reducing $A$ does not preserve eigenvalues; always work with $\det(A - \lambda I)$ for the original matrix.

blocks.html: For each eigenvalue, the eigenvectors (together with $\mathbf{0}$) form a subspace. How big that subspace is decides a great deal, as the next topic will show. We find eigenvalues with the characteristic equation and then their eigenvectors by row reduction.

On an eigenspace the matrix acts very simply: every vector in $E_\lambda$ is just multiplied by $\lambda$. A line eigenspace is a line the matrix stretches; a plane eigenspace is a whole plane the matrix stretches uniformly.

The eigenspace of $A$ for $\lambda$ is $E_\lambda = \operatorname{Nul}(A - \lambda I)$: all eigenvectors for $\lambda$ plus the zero vector. Its dimension is the geometric multiplicity of $\lambda$. The geometric multiplicity is always at least $1$ and at most the algebraic multiplicity.

blocks.title: An eigenspace that is only a line
blocks.q: For $B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ (eigenvalues $2, 2, 1$), find a basis of $E_2$.
steps: Two pivots, one free variable: $x_1 = 0$, $x_2 = x_3 = t$.
So $\lambda = 2$ has algebraic multiplicity 2 but geometric multiplicity only 1.

blocks.title: An eigenspace that is a plane
blocks.q: For $C = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ (lower triangular, eigenvalues $3, 3, 1$), find a basis of $E_3$.
steps: $E_3$ is a plane with basis $\{(-2, 1, 0), (2, 0, 1)\}$: geometric multiplicity 2, equal to the algebraic multiplicity.

blocks.html: Why must eigenvectors for different eigenvalues be independent? Take two: $A\mathbf{u} = \lambda\mathbf{u}$, $A\mathbf{v} = \mu\mathbf{v}$, $\lambda eq \mu$. Suppose $a\mathbf{u} + b\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$. Apply $A$: $a\lambda\mathbf{u} + b\mu\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$. Subtract $\lambda$ times the first equation: $b(\mu - \lambda)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$. Since $\mu eq \lambda$ and $\mathbf{v} eq \mathbf{0}$, $b = 0$; then $a\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}$ gives $a = 0$. The same idea works for any number of distinct eigenvalues. So bases of different eigenspaces put together stay independent.

blocks.cap: The shear $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ has eigenvalue 1 twice but only one eigenvector line. Choose "Stretch" or "Identity" to compare: for $2I$, every vector is an eigenvector.

blocks.html: A practical routine for a whole matrix: (1) find the eigenvalues from $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$ and note their multiplicities; (2) for each eigenvalue, row reduce $A - \lambda I$; (3) count the free variables to get the dimension and read off one basis vector per free variable. If a row reduction of $A - \lambda I$ ever shows a pivot in every column, that $\lambda$ was not an eigenvalue after all: go back and check the characteristic polynomial.

Each eigenvalue $\lambda$ has an eigenspace $\operatorname{Nul}(A - \lambda I)$; find its basis by row reduction. Its dimension (geometric multiplicity) is between 1 and the algebraic multiplicity, and eigenvectors from different eigenvalues are independent.

blocks.html: A diagonal matrix is the easiest kind of matrix: it just stretches each coordinate axis. If a matrix has enough eigenvectors, then in the basis made of those eigenvectors it is diagonal. Writing that down is diagonalization.

$A$ ($n \times n$) is diagonalizable if $A = PDP^{-1}$ with $D$ diagonal. This happens exactly when $A$ has $n$ linearly independent eigenvectors; then the columns of $P$ are those eigenvectors and the diagonal of $D$ holds their eigenvalues, in the same order.

Write $P = [\,\mathbf{v}_1\ \cdots\ \mathbf{v}_n\,]$ and $D = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n)$. Column by column, $AP = [\,A\mathbf{v}_1\ \cdots\ A\mathbf{v}_n\,]$ and $PD$ $= [\,\lambda_1\mathbf{v}_1\ \cdots\ \lambda_n\mathbf{v}_n\,]$. So $AP = PD$ says exactly that each $\mathbf{v}_i$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $\lambda_i$. If the $\mathbf{v}_i$ are independent, $P$ is invertible and $A = PDP^{-1}$. In words: change to eigenvector coordinates ($P^{-1}$), stretch each axis ($D$), change back ($P$).

blocks.title: Diagonalizing a 2 × 2 matrix
blocks.q: Diagonalize $A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$.

blocks.name: matrix2d

opts.task: Press "Apply A" and follow the two dashed lines: points on them only slide along their line.

blocks.cap: In the basis of the two eigenvector lines, $A$ is just "stretch by 5 along one line, by 2 along the other".

blocks.text: When it works, and when it does not

items: $n$ distinct eigenvalues: always diagonalizable (eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are independent).
A repeated eigenvalue: diagonalizable exactly when each eigenspace's dimension equals that eigenvalue's algebraic multiplicity, so the eigenspace dimensions add up to $n$.

blocks.title: A repeated eigenvalue that is fine
blocks.q: Is $C = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ diagonalizable?
steps: From the previous topic, $E_3$ has basis $(-2, 1, 0), (2, 0, 1)$ (dimension 2), and $E_1$ is spanned by $(0, 0, 1)$.

blocks.title: One that fails
blocks.q: Is $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ diagonalizable?
steps: $A - 2I = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ has rank 1, so $E_2$ is only a line (spanned by $(1, 0)$).
Only one independent eigenvector for a $2 \times 2$ matrix: not diagonalizable.

blocks.html: The payoff comes in the next topics: powers $A^{k} = PD^{k}P^{-1}$, long-run behavior, and systems of differential equations, which split into separate one-variable equations in eigenvector coordinates. Whenever a problem involves applying the same matrix again and again, diagonalizing first is the natural move.

Thinking a repeated eigenvalue always prevents diagonalizing, or never does. Both happen: $3I$ and the matrix $C$ above are diagonalizable, the shear is not. Decide by computing the dimension of each repeated eigenvalue's eigenspace. Distinct eigenvalues are the safe case.

blocks.html: Many processes repeat the same linear step: populations from year to year, money in accounts, customers switching brands. After $k$ steps the state is $A^{k}\mathbf{x}_0$. Diagonalization makes $A^{k}$ easy to compute and, better, easy to understand.
If $A = PDP^{-1}$, then $A^{k} = PD^{k}P^{-1}$, and $D^{k}$ just raises each diagonal entry to the power $k$. In the long run, the largest eigenvalues dominate.

$A^{2}$ $= (PDP^{-1})(PDP^{-1})$ $= PD(P^{-1}P)DP^{-1}$ $= PD^{2}P^{-1}$, because $P^{-1}P = I$ in the middle. The same cancellation happens in every power. In eigenvector coordinates, each step just multiplies coordinate $i$ by $\lambda_i$; after $k$ steps, by $\lambda_i^{k}$. Coordinates with $|\lambda_i| > 1$ grow, those with $|\lambda_i| < 1$ fade away.

blocks.title: A third power
blocks.q: Compute $A^{3}$ for $A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$ using $P = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$ and $D = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$.
steps: Check one entry the slow way: $A^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 18 & 7 \\ 14 & 11 \end{bmatrix}$, and row 1 of $A^{2}$ times column 1 of $A$ is $(18)(4) + (7)(2) = 86$. ✓

blocks.html: A Markov matrix (stochastic matrix) has nonnegative entries and columns that add up to $1$. Entry $(i, j)$ is the probability of moving from state $j$ to state $i$ in one step. A probability vector $\mathbf{x}_k$ lists the chances (or shares) of each state, and $\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = P\mathbf{x}_k$. A steady state is a probability vector $\mathbf{q}$ with $P\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}$: an eigenvector for $\lambda = 1$.

blocks.title: A two-state chain
blocks.q: Each year 10% of a city's downtown residents move to the suburbs and 20% of suburban residents move downtown. Find the long-run split.
steps: Order the states (downtown, suburbs). Column 1 is where downtown people go: $0.9$ stay, $0.1$ leave. So $P = \begin{bmatrix} 0.9 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.8 \end{bmatrix}$.
Steady state: $(P - I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}$ with $P - I = \begin{bmatrix} -0.1 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & -0.2 \end{bmatrix}$. Both rows say $q_1 = 2q_2$.
So $\mathbf{q}$ is a multiple of $(2, 1)$; make the entries add to $1$: $\mathbf{q} = \left(\frac{2}{3}, \frac{1}{3}\right)$.
blocks.a: Two thirds downtown, one third in the suburbs.

blocks.html: Why does every Markov matrix have the eigenvalue $1$, and why does the chain settle down? The columns of $P$ add to $1$, so $(1, 1, \dots, 1)P = (1, 1, \dots, 1)$: the all-ones vector is an eigenvector of $P^{T}$ for $1$, and $P$ and $P^{T}$ have the same eigenvalues. For this $P$ the other eigenvalue is $\operatorname{tr} P - 1 = 0.7$. Writing $\mathbf{x}_0 = \mathbf{q} + c\mathbf{w}$ in eigenvectors, $\mathbf{x}_k = \mathbf{q} + c(0.7)^{k}\mathbf{w} \to \mathbf{q}$, whatever the starting split.

blocks.cap: The Markov matrix keeps the steady-state direction $(2, 1)$ fixed ($\lambda = 1$) and shrinks the direction $(1, -1)$ by $0.7$ each step.

blocks.html: The steady state does not depend on the start. For larger chains with all entries of some power $P^{k}$ positive (a regular chain), the same is true: $P^{k}\mathbf{x}_0 \to \mathbf{q}$ for every probability vector $\mathbf{x}_0$.

blocks.html: A rotation by $90^\circ$ turns every direction, so it has no real eigenvectors. Its characteristic equation $\lambda^{2} + 1 = 0$ still has solutions: $\lambda = \pm i$. Complex eigenvalues are the algebra's way of saying "this matrix rotates". The polar form of a complex number tells us how much.
A real polynomial's complex roots come in conjugate pairs, so a real $2 \times 2$ matrix with a negative discriminant has eigenvalues $a \pm bi$ with $b \neq 0$.

blocks.title: Complex eigenvalues
blocks.q: Find the eigenvalues of $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$.

blocks.html: The matrix $C = \begin{bmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a \end{bmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $a \pm bi$ (its characteristic polynomial is $(a - \lambda)^{2} + b^{2}$). Write $a + bi = r(\cos\varphi + i\sin\varphi)$ with $r = \sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2}}$. Then $$C = r\begin{bmatrix} \cos\varphi & -\sin\varphi \\ \sin\varphi & \cos\varphi \end{bmatrix},$$ a rotation by $\varphi$ followed by scaling by $r$. It does to vectors in the plane exactly what multiplying by $a + bi$ does to complex numbers.

steps: It has the form $\begin{bmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a \end{bmatrix}$ with $a = 1$, $b = 1$: eigenvalues $1 \pm i$.
So $A$ rotates by $45^\circ$ and stretches by $\sqrt{2}$. Repeating it makes points spiral outward.

blocks.html: Why does every real $2 \times 2$ matrix with eigenvalues $a \pm bi$ behave like a rotation-scaling? Take a complex eigenvector $\mathbf{v}$ for $\lambda = a - bi$ and split it into real and imaginary parts. With $P = [\,\operatorname{Re}\mathbf{v}\ \ \operatorname{Im}\mathbf{v}\,]$, one can show $A = PCP^{-1}$ with $C = \begin{bmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a \end{bmatrix}$. So in the right (slanted) coordinates, $A$ is a rotation-scaling: points move on ellipses, spiraling out if $r > 1$, in if $r < 1$, and staying on closed loops if $r = 1$.

blocks.title: A complex eigenvector
blocks.q: Find an eigenvector of $C = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ for $\lambda = 2 - 3i$.
steps: Check row 2: $3 + (3i)(i) = 3 - 3 = 0$. ✓ The eigenvector for the conjugate $2 + 3i$ is the conjugate vector $(1, -i)$.

blocks.html: The same idea appears in differential equations: a system whose matrix has eigenvalues $a \pm bi$ produces oscillations with frequency $b$ that grow or decay like $e^{at}$.

Concluding "no eigenvalues" when the discriminant is negative. Over the real numbers there are no eigenvectors, but the eigenvalues exist as complex numbers, and they carry real information: $|\lambda|$ is the scale factor and the angle of $\lambda$ is the rotation.

Complex eigenvalues $a \pm bi$ of a real $2 \times 2$ matrix mean rotation: the matrix acts, in suitable coordinates, like multiplication by $a + bi$, rotating by $\arg(a + bi)$ and scaling by $|a + bi|$.

blocks.html: Diagonalization rewrote $A$ as $PDP^{-1}$. The same move with any invertible $P$ gives another matrix that describes the same map, just in different coordinates.

$A$ and $B$ are similar if $B = P^{-1}AP$ for some invertible $P$. As in change of basis, if the columns of $P$ form a basis $\mathcal{B}$, then $B$ is the matrix of $\mathbf{x} \mapsto A\mathbf{x}$ in $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates. Diagonalizable means similar to a diagonal matrix.

Similar matrices describe one linear map in two bases, so they share everything that does not depend on coordinates: the characteristic polynomial, the eigenvalues (with multiplicities), the determinant, the trace and the rank.

$\det(B - \lambda I)$ $= \det(P^{-1}AP - \lambda P^{-1}P)$ $= \det\big(P^{-1}(A - \lambda I)P\big)$ $= \det P^{-1}\det(A - \lambda I)\det P$ $= \det(A - \lambda I)$, since $\det P^{-1}\det P = 1$. Same characteristic polynomial, so the same eigenvalues; its constant term and its $\lambda^{n-1}$ coefficient give the same determinant and trace.

blocks.title: Computing a similar matrix
blocks.q: Compute $B = P^{-1}AP$ for $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ and $P = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$.
steps: Check the invariants: $\operatorname{tr} A = 1 = \operatorname{tr} B$ and $\det A = -6 = \det B$. $B$ is triangular, so its eigenvalues are $3$ and $-2$, and so are $A$'s.

blocks.html: To show two matrices are not similar, it is enough to find one invariant that differs: a different trace, determinant, rank or set of eigenvalues settles it at once. To show they are similar, you usually exhibit $P$, or show both are similar to the same diagonal matrix.

blocks.title: Same eigenvalues, not similar
blocks.q: Are $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ and $2I$ similar?
steps: Both have eigenvalues $2, 2$, trace $4$ and determinant $4$.
But $P^{-1}(2I)P = 2P^{-1}P = 2I$ for every $P$: the only matrix similar to $2I$ is $2I$ itself.
$A \neq 2I$, so they are not similar. (Indeed $A$ has only one eigenvector line, while every vector is an eigenvector of $2I$.)

blocks.html: Concluding that two matrices are similar because their eigenvalues match. Matching invariants is necessary, not sufficient. It is enough when both matrices are diagonalizable, for example when the shared eigenvalues are all distinct: then both are similar to the same diagonal matrix, and so to each other.

blocks.name: matrix2d
blocks.cap: The map $A$ stretches by $3$ and by $-2$ along its two eigenvector lines. Any matrix similar to $A$ does the same stretching along lines in other positions.

blocks.html: Similarity also explains why diagonalizing helps: if $B = P^{-1}AP$, then $B^{k} = P^{-1}A^{k}P$, so powers, and anything built from powers, can be computed in whichever basis is easiest and translated back. Choosing $P$ to make $B$ as simple as possible is the main strategy for understanding a linear map.
Similarity is what "the same up to a change of coordinates" means. Every square matrix is similar to a nearly diagonal one called its Jordan form; the shear above is already in that form.

blocks.html: The dot product measured angles between arrows in the plane. The same formula works in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and brings geometry (length, distance, right angles) into every dimension. This unit builds on it all the way to data fitting.

For $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, the inner product (dot product) is $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}$ $= \mathbf{u}^{T}\mathbf{v}$ $= u_1v_1 + \cdots + u_nv_n$. The length (norm) is $\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert = \sqrt{\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v}}$, the distance between $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ is $\lVert\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}\rVert$, and a unit vector has length $1$: dividing any nonzero $\mathbf{v}$ by its length gives the unit vector in its direction.
$\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are orthogonal (perpendicular) when $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 0$.

Why does a zero dot product mean a right angle, even in $\mathbb{R}^{10}$? Expand $\lVert\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}\rVert^{2}$ $= (\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v})\cdot(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v})$ $= \lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert^{2} + \lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert^{2} + 2\,\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}$. The Pythagorean theorem $\lVert\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}\rVert^{2}$ $= \lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert^{2} + \lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert^{2}$, which is what "right angle" means for the triangle with legs $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$, holds exactly when $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 0$. More generally $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = \lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert\cos\theta$.

blocks.html: A set of vectors is orthogonal if every pair in it is orthogonal. Nonzero orthogonal vectors are automatically independent: if $c_1\mathbf{u}_1 + \cdots + c_p\mathbf{u}_p = \mathbf{0}$, dot both sides with $\mathbf{u}_1$; every term but the first vanishes, leaving $c_1\lVert\mathbf{u}_1\rVert^{2} = 0$, so $c_1 = 0$, and likewise for every $c_i$. That is why orthogonal bases are so convenient: each weight can be found by one dot product.

In higher dimensions the dot product is just as concrete. Two survey answers, two documents' word counts, or two days of stock returns are vectors in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$, and the angle between them (through $\cos\theta = \frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert}$) is a standard measure of how similar they are. Orthogonal means "no overlap at all".

Forgetting the square root in the length, or taking the square root of each entry separately. $\lVert(3, 4)\rVert = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5$, not $3 + 4 = 7$ and not $9 + 16 = 25$. Check: the length is never less than the size of any single entry.

The rules $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{u}$, $(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v})\cdot\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{w} + \mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{w}$, $(c\mathbf{u})\cdot\mathbf{v} = c(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})$ and $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{u} > 0$ for $\mathbf{u} \neq \mathbf{0}$ are all that the arguments in this unit use.

blocks.html: A vector can be orthogonal to a whole subspace: perpendicular to every vector in it. Collecting all such vectors gives another subspace, and for a matrix this links the row space to the null space.

For a subspace $W$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$, the orthogonal complement $W^{\perp}$ is the set of all $\mathbf{z}$ with $\mathbf{z}\cdot\mathbf{w} = 0$ for every $\mathbf{w}$ in $W$. To test membership it is enough to check a spanning set of $W$: if $\mathbf{z}$ is orthogonal to each $\mathbf{w}_i$, it is orthogonal to every combination of them.
$(\operatorname{Row} A)^{\perp} = \operatorname{Nul} A$ and $(\operatorname{Col} A)^{\perp} = \operatorname{Nul} A^{T}$. Also $\dim W + \dim W^{\perp} = n$.

$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ says, row by row, that (row $i$ of $A$)$\cdot\mathbf{x} = 0$ for each $i$. So $\mathbf{x}$ solves $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ exactly when it is orthogonal to every row, and so to every combination of rows: $\operatorname{Nul} A = (\operatorname{Row} A)^{\perp}$. Applying this to $A^{T}$, whose rows are the columns of $A$, gives the second statement. The dimension count is rank–nullity: if $W = \operatorname{Row} A$ has dimension $r$, then $\dim \operatorname{Nul} A = n - r$.

blocks.html: Two more facts: $W \cap W^{\perp} = \{\mathbf{0}\}$ (a vector orthogonal to itself has $\mathbf{z}\cdot\mathbf{z} = 0$, so it is $\mathbf{0}$), and $(W^{\perp})^{\perp} = W$. Together with the dimension count they say that $\mathbb{R}^n$ splits cleanly into $W$ and $W^{\perp}$: every vector is a piece in $W$ plus a piece in $W^{\perp}$, which is the next topic.

blocks.html: What is the closest point of a subspace to a given vector? In the plane, drop a perpendicular. In any dimension, the answer is the orthogonal projection, and it rests on the splitting $\mathbb{R}^n = W \oplus W^{\perp}$ from orthogonal complements and on a basis of $W$.

Onto a line. The projection of $\mathbf{y}$ onto the line through $\mathbf{u}$ is $$\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \frac{\mathbf{y}\cdot\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{u}}\mathbf{u},$$ and $\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is orthogonal to $\mathbf{u}$ (check: $\mathbf{z}\cdot\mathbf{u}$ $= \mathbf{y}\cdot\mathbf{u} - \frac{\mathbf{y}\cdot\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{u}}\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{u}$ $= 0$).

If $\{\mathbf{u}_1, \dots, \mathbf{u}_p\}$ is an orthogonal basis of $W$, the projection of $\mathbf{y}$ onto $W$ is $$\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \frac{\mathbf{y}\cdot\mathbf{u}_1}{\mathbf{u}_1\cdot\mathbf{u}_1}\mathbf{u}_1 + \cdots + \frac{\mathbf{y}\cdot\mathbf{u}_p}{\mathbf{u}_p\cdot\mathbf{u}_p}\mathbf{u}_p.$$ Then $\mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is in $W^{\perp}$, and $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is the point of $W$ closest to $\mathbf{y}$.

Why closest? Take any $\mathbf{v}$ in $W$. Then $\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{v}$ $= (\mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}) + (\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{v})$. The first piece is in $W^{\perp}$ and the second is in $W$, so they are orthogonal and the Pythagorean theorem gives $\lVert\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{v}\rVert^{2}$ $= \lVert\mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}\rVert^{2} + \lVert\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{v}\rVert^{2}$. That is smallest exactly when $\mathbf{v} = \hat{\mathbf{y}}$. And why does the formula give a vector with $\mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}$ in $W^{\perp}$? Dot $\mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}$ with $\mathbf{u}_1$: because $\mathbf{u}_1\cdot\mathbf{u}_j = 0$ for $j \neq 1$, only the first term of $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ survives, and it cancels $\mathbf{y}\cdot\mathbf{u}_1$ exactly.

Example: $W$ = the $xy$-plane with basis $(1, 0, 0)$, $(1, 1, 0)$ and $\mathbf{y} = (0, 2, 1)$. The true projection is $(0, 2, 0)$, but the separate projections are $(0, 0, 0)$ and $(1, 1, 0)$, which add to $(1, 1, 0)$: wrong. Fix it by making the basis orthogonal first (Gram–Schmidt) or by solving the normal equations of least squares. Check: $\mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}$ must be orthogonal to every basis vector.

blocks.html: Projections are easy with an orthogonal basis and awkward without one. The Gram–Schmidt process turns any basis into an orthogonal one, spanning the same subspace, by removing the overlap one vector at a time.

Given a basis $\mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_p$: set $\mathbf{v}_1 = \mathbf{x}_1$, and for each next vector subtract its projections onto the vectors already built: $$\mathbf{v}_k = \mathbf{x}_k - \frac{\mathbf{x}_k\cdot\mathbf{v}_1}{\mathbf{v}_1\cdot\mathbf{v}_1}\mathbf{v}_1 - \cdots - \frac{\mathbf{x}_k\cdot\mathbf{v}_{k-1}}{\mathbf{v}_{k-1}\cdot\mathbf{v}_{k-1}}\mathbf{v}_{k-1}.$$ Then $\{\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_p\}$ is an orthogonal basis of the same subspace. Divide each by its length for an orthonormal basis.

At step $k$, $\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_{k-1}$ are orthogonal and span the same space as $\mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_{k-1}$. The subtracted part is the projection of $\mathbf{x}_k$ onto that space (the orthogonal-basis formula), so what remains, $\mathbf{v}_k$, is orthogonal to all of it. It is not $\mathbf{0}$, because $\mathbf{x}_k$ is not in the span of the earlier $\mathbf{x}$'s. And $\mathbf{v}_k$ is $\mathbf{x}_k$ minus a combination of earlier vectors, so the span does not change.

blocks.q: Apply Gram–Schmidt to $\mathbf{x}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{x}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$, then normalize.
steps: Scaling does not change orthogonality, so use $\mathbf{v}_2 = (1, -1, 2)$ to avoid fractions. Check: $\mathbf{v}_1\cdot\mathbf{v}_2 = 1 - 1 + 0 = 0$. ✓

blocks.html: Run Gram–Schmidt on the columns of an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ with independent columns, normalize, and put the results in the columns of $Q$. Each $\mathbf{x}_k$ is a combination of $\mathbf{q}_1, \dots, \mathbf{q}_k$ only, so $A = QR$ with $R$ upper triangular (and positive diagonal). Since $Q^{T}Q = I$, the triangle is easy to find: $R = Q^{T}A$.

blocks.html: For three vectors the pattern continues: $\mathbf{v}_3$ $= \mathbf{x}_3 - \frac{\mathbf{x}_3\cdot\mathbf{v}_1}{\mathbf{v}_1\cdot\mathbf{v}_1}\mathbf{v}_1 - \frac{\mathbf{x}_3\cdot\mathbf{v}_2}{\mathbf{v}_2\cdot\mathbf{v}_2}\mathbf{v}_2$. Each new vector costs one more projection. If some $\mathbf{v}_k$ comes out as $\mathbf{0}$, then $\mathbf{x}_k$ was a combination of the earlier vectors: the input was not independent, and you can simply drop it.

Subtracting projections onto the original $\mathbf{x}$'s instead of the new $\mathbf{v}$'s. The formula only works with the orthogonal vectors built so far. Check each new vector by dotting it with all earlier ones: every dot product must be $0$.
Computers use QR to solve least-squares problems, because it avoids forming $A^{T}A$, which can lose accuracy.

blocks.html: Real data rarely fit a model exactly. In Algebra 1 you drew a line of fit and looked at residuals; here we find the best line exactly. In matrix language: $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has no solution, so we look for the $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ that makes $A\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ as close as possible to $\mathbf{b}$. Projection gives the answer.

A least-squares solution of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ minimizes $\lVert\mathbf{b} - A\mathbf{x}\rVert$. The least-squares solutions are exactly the solutions of the normal equations $$A^{T}A\hat{\mathbf{x}} = A^{T}\mathbf{b}.$$ When the columns of $A$ are independent, $\hat{\mathbf{x}} = (A^{T}A)^{-1}A^{T}\mathbf{b}$ is unique.

$A\mathbf{x}$ ranges over $\operatorname{Col} A$, so the closest $A\mathbf{x}$ to $\mathbf{b}$ is the projection $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ of $\mathbf{b}$ onto $\operatorname{Col} A$. The leftover $\mathbf{b} - A\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ must be orthogonal to $\operatorname{Col} A$, so it lies in $(\operatorname{Col} A)^{\perp} = \operatorname{Nul} A^{T}$ (from orthogonal complements): $A^{T}(\mathbf{b} - A\hat{\mathbf{x}}) = \mathbf{0}$. Rearranged, that is $A^{T}A\hat{\mathbf{x}} = A^{T}\mathbf{b}$. No orthogonal basis is needed: the normal equations do the projection for us.

blocks.name: la-proj
blocks.cap: $\mathbf{b}$ is not in $\operatorname{Col} A$ (the plane). The best we can do is $A\hat{\mathbf{x}}$, its projection; the residual $\mathbf{b} - A\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ is perpendicular to the plane.

blocks.title: An inconsistent system
blocks.q: Find the least-squares solution of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ with $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix}$.

steps: Each point gives an equation $\beta_0 + \beta_1x_i = y_i$. The design matrix has a column of $1$s and a column of $x$'s: $X = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{y} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 3 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$.
The line is $y = 0.8 + 0.8x$. Its residuals $(0.2, -0.6, 0.6, -0.2)$ add up to $0$, as they always do when the model has an intercept.

blocks.name: scatter
blocks.cap: The least-squares line makes the total area of the residual squares as small as possible. Drag a point and watch it refit.

blocks.html: Trying to solve $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ directly when it is inconsistent, for example by row reducing $[\,A \mid \mathbf{b}\,]$, finding a $0 = c$ row, and stopping, or by solving just two of the equations and ignoring the rest. Multiply by $A^{T}$ first and solve the normal equations. Check: the residual $\mathbf{b} - A\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ must be orthogonal to every column of $A$.

This is exactly ordinary least squares (OLS) in statistics and economics. With many explanatory variables, the design matrix $X$ gets one column per variable, and the estimate is $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (X^{T}X)^{-1}X^{T}\mathbf{y}$. The Teddy Rook Book Econometrics course builds on this formula, starting with fitting a line and multiple regression.

blocks.html: Gram–Schmidt produces orthonormal columns. Square matrices with orthonormal columns are the rigid motions of linear algebra: rotations and reflections. They are the easiest matrices to invert and they never distort lengths.

A square matrix $Q$ is orthogonal when its columns are orthonormal, that is, $Q^{T}Q = I$. Then $Q^{-1} = Q^{T}$, and $Q$ preserves lengths and angles: $\lVert Q\mathbf{x}\rVert = \lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert$ and $(Q\mathbf{x})\cdot(Q\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{y}$.

Entry $(i, j)$ of $Q^{T}Q$ is (column $i$)$\cdot$(column $j$). Orthonormal columns make this $1$ when $i = j$ and $0$ otherwise: $Q^{T}Q = I$. For a square matrix, a one-sided inverse is the inverse, so $Q^{-1} = Q^{T}$. Then $(Q\mathbf{x})\cdot(Q\mathbf{y})$ $= (Q\mathbf{x})^{T}(Q\mathbf{y})$ $= \mathbf{x}^{T}Q^{T}Q\mathbf{y}$ $= \mathbf{x}^{T}\mathbf{y}$. Dot products are kept, so lengths and angles are kept.

blocks.title: Checking and inverting
blocks.q: Show that $Q = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{3} & \frac{2}{3} & \frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} & -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} & -\frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} \end{bmatrix}$ is orthogonal and find $Q^{-1}$.
steps: Column lengths: $\frac{1}{9}(1 + 4 + 4) = 1$, and the same for the others.
Column 1 $\cdot$ column 2 $= \frac{1}{9}(2 + 2 - 4) = 0$; similarly the other pairs. So $Q^{T}Q = I$.
$Q^{-1} = Q^{T}$. This $Q$ happens to be symmetric, so $Q^{-1} = Q$: applying it twice gives the identity (it is a reflection).

steps: The second column must be a unit vector perpendicular to $\left(\frac{3}{5}, \frac{4}{5}\right)$: either $\left(-\frac{4}{5}, \frac{3}{5}\right)$ or $\left(\frac{4}{5}, -\frac{3}{5}\right)$.
Determinant with the first choice: $\frac{3}{5}\cdot\frac{3}{5} - \left(-\frac{4}{5}\right)\frac{4}{5} = 1$. ✓ (The second choice gives $-1$, a reflection.)

blocks.cap: An orthogonal matrix moves the grid rigidly: lengths, angles and areas are unchanged ($\det Q = \pm 1$).

items: Every $2 \times 2$ orthogonal matrix is a rotation $\begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}$ (determinant $1$) or a reflection $\begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & \sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & -\cos\theta \end{bmatrix}$ (determinant $-1$).
$\det Q = \pm 1$, because $(\det Q)^{2} = \det Q^{T}\det Q = \det I = 1$.
Products of orthogonal matrices are orthogonal: $(Q_1Q_2)^{T}(Q_1Q_2)$ $= Q_2^{T}Q_1^{T}Q_1Q_2$ $= I$.

blocks.html: Because $Q^{-1} = Q^{T}$, solving $Q\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ costs only a multiplication: $\mathbf{x} = Q^{T}\mathbf{b}$, so each coordinate is a dot product $\mathbf{q}_i\cdot\mathbf{b}$. This is the projection formula again: an orthonormal basis gives coordinates for free.

Calling a matrix orthogonal because its columns are perpendicular. They must also have length $1$. $\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -4 \\ 4 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$ has perpendicular columns of length $5$, so $Q^{T}Q = 25I$, not $I$; dividing by $5$ fixes it.

Rectangular matrices can have orthonormal columns too. If $U$ is $m \times n$ with orthonormal columns, then still $U^{T}U = I_n$ and $\lVert U\mathbf{x}\rVert = \lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert$, but $UU^{T}$ is not $I_m$: it is the projection onto the column space of $U$. The $Q$ in a QR factorization is usually of this kind.
Orthogonal matrices are prized in computing: multiplying by them never magnifies rounding errors, which is why QR and the SVD are built from them.

blocks.html: Most matrices need care to diagonalize: eigenvalues may be complex, eigenvectors may be missing, and $P$ may be awkward to invert. Symmetric matrices ($A^{T} = A$) have none of these problems. Their eigenvectors can be chosen orthonormal, so $P^{-1}$ is just $P^{T}$.

Spectral theorem. A real $n \times n$ matrix $A$ is symmetric exactly when it is orthogonally diagonalizable: $A = PDP^{T}$ with $P$ orthogonal and $D$ diagonal. Its eigenvalues are real, and eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are orthogonal.

The orthogonality is a two-line proof. Let $A\mathbf{u} = \lambda\mathbf{u}$ and $A\mathbf{v} = \mu\mathbf{v}$ with $\lambda \neq \mu$. Then $\lambda(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})$ $= (A\mathbf{u})\cdot\mathbf{v}$ $= (A\mathbf{u})^{T}\mathbf{v}$ $= \mathbf{u}^{T}A^{T}\mathbf{v}$ $= \mathbf{u}^{T}A\mathbf{v}$ $= \mu(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})$, using $A^{T} = A$. So $(\lambda - \mu)\,\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 0$, which forces $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 0$. The other direction is quick too: $(PDP^{T})^{T} = PD^{T}P^{T} = PDP^{T}$. (That the eigenvalues are real, and that repeated eigenvalues still have full eigenspaces, takes a longer argument that we do not repeat here.)

blocks.title: Orthogonally diagonalize
blocks.q: Orthogonally diagonalize $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$.
steps: They are orthogonal, as promised: $(1)(2) + (2)(-1) = 0$. Divide each by its length $\sqrt{5}$.

blocks.html: Writing $A = PDP^{T}$ column by column gives the spectral decomposition $$A = \lambda_1\mathbf{u}_1\mathbf{u}_1^{T} + \lambda_2\mathbf{u}_2\mathbf{u}_2^{T} + \cdots + \lambda_n\mathbf{u}_n\mathbf{u}_n^{T}.$$ Each $\mathbf{u}_i\mathbf{u}_i^{T}$ is the projection onto the line through $\mathbf{u}_i$, so a symmetric matrix is a weighted sum of projections onto perpendicular lines.

blocks.html: Geometrically, a symmetric matrix does the simplest thing a linear map can do: it picks $n$ perpendicular directions and stretches (or flips) along each one, with no turning or shearing in between. A general matrix may also rotate; the next topics show how the SVD separates the stretching from the rotating for every matrix.

Symmetric matrices are everywhere: covariance matrices in statistics, the Hessian of second derivatives in calculus, stiffness matrices in engineering, and $A^{T}A$ for any matrix $A$, which is the door to the SVD.
Forgetting to normalize. The columns of $P$ must be unit eigenvectors; otherwise $P^{T} \neq P^{-1}$ and $PDP^{T}$ is not $A$. Check: $P^{T}P$ should be $I$.

blocks.html: Expressions like $5x_1^{2} + 4x_1x_2 + 2x_2^{2}$ appear whenever we measure energy, variance or curvature. Every such expression is $\mathbf{x}^{T}A\mathbf{x}$ for a symmetric matrix $A$, and the spectral theorem tells us exactly what it looks like.

A quadratic form on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is $Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^{T}A\mathbf{x}$ with $A$ symmetric. The diagonal entries of $A$ are the coefficients of the squares, and each cross term's coefficient is split evenly between two off-diagonal entries: $$5x_1^{2} + 4x_1x_2 + 2x_2^{2} = \mathbf{x}^{T}\begin{bmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\mathbf{x}.$$

Principal axes. With $A = PDP^{T}$ and new coordinates $\mathbf{y} = P^{T}\mathbf{x}$, $Q = \lambda_1y_1^{2} + \cdots + \lambda_ny_n^{2}$: no cross terms. So $Q$ is positive definite ($Q(\mathbf{x}) > 0$ for all $\mathbf{x} \neq \mathbf{0}$) exactly when every eigenvalue of $A$ is positive, negative definite when all are negative, and indefinite when there are eigenvalues of both signs.

$\mathbf{x}^{T}A\mathbf{x}$ $= \mathbf{x}^{T}PDP^{T}\mathbf{x}$ $= (P^{T}\mathbf{x})^{T}D(P^{T}\mathbf{x})$ $= \mathbf{y}^{T}D\mathbf{y}$ $= \sum \lambda_iy_i^{2}$. Since $P$ is invertible, $\mathbf{x} \neq \mathbf{0}$ exactly when $\mathbf{y} \neq \mathbf{0}$. If every $\lambda_i > 0$, the sum is positive for every nonzero $\mathbf{y}$. If some $\lambda_i \leq 0$, choose $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{e}_i$ to get $Q = \lambda_i \leq 0$. Geometrically, the eigenvectors are the axes of the level curves $Q = c$ (ellipses or hyperbolas).

blocks.title: Classify a form
blocks.q: Classify $Q = 5x_1^{2} + 4x_1x_2 + 2x_2^{2}$ and find its principal-axes form.
steps: Both eigenvalues positive: positive definite. Every level curve $Q = c > 0$ is an ellipse.
Unit eigenvectors: $\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(2, 1)$ for $6$ and $\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(-1, 2)$ for $1$. In those coordinates $Q = 6y_1^{2} + y_2^{2}$.

steps: One positive, one negative: indefinite. For example $Q(1, 1) = 8 > 0$ and $Q(1, -1) = -4 < 0$. The graph is a saddle.

blocks.cap: The graph of $Q = ax^2 + 2bxy + cy^2$, the form of $\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ b & c \end{bmatrix}$. Positive definite gives a bowl; change $b$ until $ac - b^2 < 0$ and it becomes a saddle.

blocks.html: For a $2 \times 2$ matrix $\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ b & c \end{bmatrix}$ there is a shortcut: the product of the eigenvalues is $\det A = ac - b^{2}$ and their sum is $a + c$. So $Q$ is positive definite exactly when $a > 0$ and $ac - b^{2} > 0$. This is the test behind the second derivative test in multivariable calculus, where $A$ is the matrix of second partial derivatives.

A positive semidefinite form ($Q \geq 0$, with some eigenvalue $0$) is flat along the eigenvectors for $0$: its graph is a trough rather than a bowl. Every matrix of the form $A^{T}A$ is positive semidefinite, since $\mathbf{x}^{T}A^{T}A\mathbf{x} = \lVert A\mathbf{x}\rVert^{2} \geq 0$, and positive definite exactly when the columns of $A$ are independent. That fact is used in the next topic.

Putting the whole cross-term coefficient in both off-diagonal spots. For $4x_1x_2$ the entries are $2$ and $2$, because $\mathbf{x}^{T}A\mathbf{x}$ picks up $a_{12}x_1x_2 + a_{21}x_2x_1$ $= 2a_{12}x_1x_2$. Check: multiply out $\mathbf{x}^{T}A\mathbf{x}$ with your matrix and compare.

blocks.html: The spectral theorem diagonalizes symmetric matrices with orthonormal eigenvectors. The singular value decomposition does something like it for every matrix, square or not: it finds orthonormal input directions that $A$ sends to orthogonal output directions.

Every $m \times n$ matrix factors as $A = U\Sigma V^{T}$, with $U$ ($m \times m$) and $V$ ($n \times n$) orthogonal and $\Sigma$ ($m \times n$) zero except for $\sigma_1 \geq \sigma_2 \geq \cdots \geq 0$ on its diagonal. The singular values $\sigma_i$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of $A^{T}A$; the columns $\mathbf{v}_i$ of $V$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A^{T}A$, and $\mathbf{u}_i = A\mathbf{v}_i/\sigma_i$ for each $\sigma_i > 0$.

$A^{T}A$ is symmetric, so it has orthonormal eigenvectors $\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_n$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_i$. They are never negative: $\lambda_i$ $= \mathbf{v}_i^{T}A^{T}A\mathbf{v}_i$ $= \lVert A\mathbf{v}_i\rVert^{2} \geq 0$. So $\lVert A\mathbf{v}_i\rVert = \sqrt{\lambda_i} = \sigma_i$. And the images are orthogonal: $(A\mathbf{v}_i)\cdot(A\mathbf{v}_j)$ $= \mathbf{v}_i^{T}A^{T}A\mathbf{v}_j$ $= \lambda_j\,\mathbf{v}_i\cdot\mathbf{v}_j$ $= 0$ for $i \neq j$. Dividing by their lengths gives orthonormal $\mathbf{u}_i$ with $A\mathbf{v}_i = \sigma_i\mathbf{u}_i$; in matrix form $AV = U\Sigma$, so $A = U\Sigma V^{T}$ (extend the $\mathbf{u}$'s to a full orthonormal basis if needed).

blocks.html: What the SVD tells you at a glance: $\operatorname{rank} A$ is the number of nonzero singular values; $\mathbf{u}_1, \dots, \mathbf{u}_r$ are an orthonormal basis of $\operatorname{Col} A$ and $\mathbf{v}_{r+1}, \dots, \mathbf{v}_n$ of $\operatorname{Nul} A$; and $\sigma_1$ is the largest stretch, $\max \lVert A\mathbf{x}\rVert$ over unit vectors $\mathbf{x}$.

steps: This shear stretches some vectors by $2.4$ and shrinks others to $0.4$ of their length, even though both eigenvalues are $1$.

blocks.html: Taking the singular values to be the eigenvalues of $A$. They agree only for special matrices (symmetric with nonnegative eigenvalues). In general use the square roots of the eigenvalues of $A^{T}A$. Checks: singular values are never negative, and for a square matrix their product is $|\det A|$.
For a wide matrix ($m < n$) it is quicker to find the eigenvalues of the smaller matrix $AA^{T}$: its nonzero eigenvalues are the same as those of $A^{T}A$.

blocks.html: The SVD sorts a matrix into pieces by importance. Keeping the important pieces and dropping the rest is the idea behind image compression, noise removal, recommendation systems and principal component analysis.

Multiplying out $U\Sigma V^{T}$ column by column gives the outer-product form $$A = \sigma_1\mathbf{u}_1\mathbf{v}_1^{T} + \sigma_2\mathbf{u}_2\mathbf{v}_2^{T} + \cdots + \sigma_r\mathbf{u}_r\mathbf{v}_r^{T},$$ a sum of rank-1 matrices, largest first. The rank-$k$ approximation $A_k$ keeps the first $k$ terms.

Eckart–Young. $A_k$ is the closest matrix of rank $k$ to $A$. The error is $\lVert A - A_k\rVert = \sigma_{k+1}$ (largest stretch) and $\lVert A - A_k\rVert_F$ $= \sqrt{\sigma_{k+1}^{2} + \cdots + \sigma_r^{2}}$ (square root of the sum of squared entries).

Why is dropping the small terms the right move? The Frobenius norm satisfies $\lVert A\rVert_F^{2} = \sigma_1^{2} + \cdots + \sigma_r^{2}$, because orthogonal matrices do not change it and $\Sigma$ holds the rest. So each term carries "energy" $\sigma_i^{2}$, and the leftover $A - A_k$ is itself an SVD with the dropped singular values. Proving that no other rank-$k$ matrix does better takes more work, but the energy count shows why the largest terms matter most.

Noise reduction: noise spreads over many small singular values; truncating removes much of it.
Least squares: the pseudoinverse $A^{+} = V\Sigma^{+}U^{T}$ gives the least-squares solution of smallest length, even when the columns are dependent.
